preamble: An Act to consolidate and amend the laws relating to the procedure of the Courts of Civil Judicature.

glossary.Code of Civil Procedure: The 1908 Act consolidating and amending the general procedure followed by civil courts in India.
glossary.tribal areas: The territories included, immediately before 21 January 1972, in the tribal areas of Assam under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.
glossary.Official Gazette: The government's official publication used to give legal notice of notifications, rules, and other statutory actions.
glossary.Sixth Schedule: The part of the Constitution providing for administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
glossary.decree: The formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines the rights of the parties on any matter in controversy in the suit; may be preliminary, final, or partly both.
glossary.decree-holder: Any person in whose favour a decree has been passed or an order capable of execution has been made.
glossary.district: The local limits of the jurisdiction of a principal civil court of original jurisdiction (a District Court), including a High Court's ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
glossary.foreign Court: A court situated outside India that is not established or continued by the authority of the Central Government.
glossary.foreign judgment: The judgment of a foreign Court.
glossary.judgment: The statement given by a Judge of the grounds of a decree or order.
glossary.legal representative: A person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, including an intermeddler with the estate and a successor on whom the estate devolves in a representative suit.
glossary.mesne profits: Profits a wrongful possessor of property actually received, or could have received with ordinary diligence, plus interest, excluding profits from the possessor's own improvements.
glossary.order: The formal expression of any decision of a civil court that is not a decree.
glossary.pleader: Any person entitled to appear and plead for another in court, including an advocate, vakil, or attorney of a High Court.
glossary.public officer: A person falling within one of eight defined categories of government, judicial, military, or local-authority service or duty under section 2(17).
glossary.District Court: The principal civil court of original jurisdiction for a district.
glossary.High Court: The highest court of civil (and other) jurisdiction in a State or Union territory, to which District Courts and subordinate courts answer.
glossary.Court of Small Causes: A court of summary civil jurisdiction constituted under the Small Cause Courts Acts to try suits of limited value quickly and cheaply.
glossary.special law: A law applicable to a particular subject matter, as distinguished from the Code's general procedure.
glossary.local law: A law applicable only to a particular part of the territory, as distinguished from a law of general application.
glossary.landlord: A person entitled to receive rent for agricultural or other land from a tenant or occupier.
glossary.agricultural land: Land used for agricultural purposes, relevant to rent-recovery remedies and Revenue Court jurisdiction.
glossary.Revenue Court: A court with jurisdiction under local law over suits/proceedings relating to rent, revenue, or profits of agricultural land, excluding an ordinary civil court exercising civil-nature jurisdiction.
glossary.pecuniary jurisdiction: The monetary ceiling on the value of a suit's subject-matter that a given court is competent to try.
glossary.subject-matter: The property, right, or relief that is the substance of the dispute in a suit.
glossary.Provincial Small Cause Courts Act: The Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, constituting Small Cause Courts outside the Presidency towns.
glossary.execution of decrees: The formal process by which a court enforces and gives practical effect to a decree or order.
glossary.Presidency Small Cause Courts: Small Cause Courts established at Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay under the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882.
glossary.Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882: The Act constituting and governing the Small Cause Courts of the Presidency towns of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay.
glossary.civil nature: The quality of a suit or right that makes it triable as a civil matter, as opposed to a purely religious, political, or non-justiciable question.
glossary.jurisdiction: The legal authority of a court to hear and decide a particular matter.
glossary.expressly barred: A statutory bar on a court's jurisdiction stated in clear, specific words in a statute.
glossary.impliedly barred: A bar on a court's jurisdiction arising from the scheme and language of a special statute, even without explicit ousting words.
glossary.stay of suit: An order halting the trial of a suit, typically pending the outcome of an earlier suit on the same matter.
glossary.same matter in issue: A fact or question directly and substantially contested and requiring decision in both the earlier and later proceeding.
glossary.previously instituted suit: A suit filed before the suit now under consideration, relevant to the section 10 stay-of-suit bar.
glossary.same title: The same legal basis or capacity under which parties claim, used to determine whether privies are bound alongside the original parties.
glossary.res judicata: The doctrine barring re-litigation of a matter directly and substantially in issue that has already been heard and finally decided between the same parties by a competent court.
glossary.former suit: For res judicata purposes, whichever of two suits was decided first, regardless of the order in which they were filed.
glossary.matter directly and substantially in iss: An issue that is a real and material point of controversy actually requiring decision in the suit, as opposed to a collateral or incidental question.
glossary.constructive res judicata: The rule that a matter which ought to have been raised as a ground of attack or defence in a former suit is deemed to have been in issue, even if never actually pleaded.
glossary.competent Court: A court legally empowered, by jurisdiction over subject-matter, value, and territory, to try and decide the suit or issue in question.
glossary.cause of action: The bundle of essential facts that a plaintiff must prove to be entitled to the relief claimed.
glossary.bar to suit: A rule or provision that prevents a party from instituting or maintaining a particular suit.
glossary.competent jurisdiction: Jurisdiction properly and validly held by a court under applicable law, including private international law standards for foreign courts.
glossary.natural justice: The basic fair-procedure requirements of a proper hearing and an unbiased decision-maker.
glossary.fraud: Deliberate deception used to obtain an unfair or unlawful advantage, including in obtaining a judgment.
glossary.international law: The body of rules governing relations between states and, here, the recognised principles applied to determine jurisdiction and recognition of foreign judgments.
glossary.presumption: A rule by which a court infers a fact to be true unless and until it is disproved by evidence to the contrary.
glossary.certified copy: An official copy of a document, authenticated as a true copy by a competent authority.
glossary.lowest grade: The court of the least seniority or jurisdictional rank that is nonetheless competent to try a given suit.
glossary.immovable property: Land and things permanently attached to land, including benefits arising out of land, but excluding standing timber, growing crops, and grass.
glossary.mortgage: A transfer of an interest in immovable property to secure the repayment of a debt or performance of an obligation.
glossary.foreclosure: A mortgagee's remedy extinguishing the mortgagor's right to redeem the mortgaged property.
glossary.redemption: A mortgagor's right to recover mortgaged property upon repayment of the secured debt.
glossary.distraint: The act of seizing property, often to enforce payment of rent or a debt.
glossary.personal obedience: Relief that can be fully satisfied by compelling a defendant's own personal act, rather than by operating directly on property.
glossary.different Courts: Two or more courts whose separate local jurisdictional limits each cover part of the property or subject-matter in suit.
glossary.cognizable: Capable of being taken up and tried by a court, having regard to its jurisdiction over the value or nature of the claim.
glossary.uncertainty of jurisdiction: A genuine doubt as to which of two or more courts has territorial jurisdiction over particular property.
glossary.recorded statement: A court's formal note, made under section 18, recording its satisfaction that jurisdictional uncertainty exists.
glossary.failure of justice: A real prejudice or injustice actually resulting from an error or irregularity, as opposed to a mere technical defect.
glossary.compensation for wrong: Monetary relief claimed for a civil wrong done to a person or to movable property.
glossary.movable property: Property other than immovable property; under the Code it expressly includes growing crops.
glossary.option of plaintiff: The plaintiff's statutory right to choose between two or more permissible venues for filing a suit.
glossary.corporation: A legal entity such as a company, deemed under section 20 to carry on business at its principal or a relevant subordinate office.
glossary.subordinate office: A branch or secondary office of a corporation, relevant for founding venue where the cause of action arises there.
glossary.leave of the Court: Formal permission granted by the court to take a procedural step, such as suing a non-local defendant jointly with a local one.
glossary.acquiescence: A party's conduct amounting to tacit consent or non-objection to a procedural step, such as the venue chosen for a suit.
glossary.objection to jurisdiction: A challenge to a court's competence to try a suit, based on place of suing, pecuniary limits, or local execution limits.
glossary.place of suing: The territorial venue in which a suit is properly instituted.
glossary.earliest possible opportunity: The first available procedural moment, generally at or before the settlement of issues, at which an objection must be raised to preserve it.
glossary.set aside decree: To annul or nullify a decree, whether by appeal, review, revision, or a separate suit where permitted.
glossary.transfer of suit: The movement of a pending suit from one court to another for trial or disposal.
glossary.notice to parties: Formal intimation given to the parties to a proceeding before an order affecting them, such as a transfer, is made.
glossary.Appellate Court: A court exercising jurisdiction to hear appeals from the decrees or orders of a subordinate court.
glossary.application for transfer: A formal request made to the appropriate court seeking transfer of a suit under sections 22-25.
glossary.transfer: The act of moving a pending suit, appeal, or proceeding from one court to another for trial or disposal.
glossary.withdrawal: The act of a superior court taking a pending suit or proceeding out of a subordinate court, for itself or further transfer.
glossary.suo motu: An action taken by a court on its own initiative, without a party's application.
glossary.proceeding: Under section 24, a term extended to include a proceeding for the execution of a decree or order, in addition to suits and appeals.
glossary.Supreme Court: The apex court of India, here exercising the power under section 25 to transfer suits, appeals, or proceedings between States.
glossary.transfer between States: The Supreme Court's power under section 25 to move litigation from a court in one State to a court in another State.
glossary.motion: A formal application made to a court, here the prescribed mode for a section 25 transfer application.
glossary.affidavit: A written statement of facts sworn to be true, used to support applications and, under section 26(2), to prove plaint facts.
glossary.frivolous application: An application devoid of merit or seriousness, attracting a possible compensatory costs order under section 25(4).
glossary.plaint: The formal written statement of a plaintiff's claim by which a civil suit is instituted.
glossary.institution of suit: The formal commencement of a suit, ordinarily by presentation of a plaint.
glossary.summons: A court process calling upon a defendant or witness to appear before the court.
glossary.duly instituted: A suit that has been properly and validly commenced in accordance with the Code's requirements.
glossary.thirty days: The outer time limit from institution of the suit within which a summons must call for the defendant's appearance under section 27.
glossary.interstate service: Service of a summons routed through a court in another State under section 28.
glossary.translation: A rendering of a document into another language, required under section 28(3) when languages of the summons and record differ.
glossary.record of proceedings: The documented history of steps taken by a court in a matter, returned along with an executed summons under section 28(2).
glossary.foreign summons: A summons or process issued by a non-Code-governed Indian court, a Central-Government-established court abroad, or a notified foreign court under section 29.
glossary.reciprocity: The mutual arrangement by which summonses from certain outside courts are served within Code territory, and vice versa.
glossary.discovery: The pre-trial process by which a party obtains disclosure of facts, documents, or objects relevant to the suit.
glossary.interrogatories: Written questions formally put by one party to another, to be answered under oath, as part of discovery.
glossary.inspection: The examination of documents or objects produced by a party for the purposes of the suit.
glossary.impounding: The court's act of retaining custody of a document produced before it.
glossary.witness summons: A summons issued to compel a person's attendance to give evidence or produce documents or objects.
glossary.warrant of arrest: A judicial order authorising the arrest of a person, here to compel attendance under section 32.
glossary.attachment of property: The seizure of a person's property by court order to compel compliance or to satisfy a decree.
glossary.fine: A monetary penalty imposed by a court, capped at five thousand rupees under section 32(c).
glossary.civil prison: A place of civil (non-criminal) detention used to enforce compliance, such as furnishing security under section 32(d).
glossary.security for appearance: A guarantee, often monetary, required from a person to ensure their future attendance before the court.
glossary.hearing: The stage at which a court considers the evidence and arguments in a case before pronouncing judgment.
glossary.interest: A sum payable on a principal amount for the use of money or as compensation for delayed payment.
glossary.principal sum: The core amount of money adjudged due in a money decree, exclusive of interest.
glossary.commercial transaction: Under section 34, a transaction connected with the industry, trade, or business of the party incurring the liability.
glossary.nationalised bank: A corresponding new bank as defined in the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970.
glossary.pendente lite interest: Interest awarded for the period from the institution of the suit to the date of the decree.
glossary.costs: Expenses of and incidental to litigation, which a court may order one party to pay to another.
glossary.discretion of the Court: The court's power to decide a matter, such as costs, based on the facts and circumstances rather than a fixed rule.
glossary.follow the event: The general costs principle that the unsuccessful party pays the costs of the successful party.
glossary.compensatory costs: Costs awarded under section 35A to compensate a party who successfully objects to a false or vexatious claim or defence.
glossary.vexatious claim: A claim made without genuine merit, known by its proponent to be false, and pursued to harass or burden the other party.
glossary.false defence: A defence raised to the knowledge of the party raising it that it is untrue.
glossary.objector: The party who raises an objection under section 35A to an opponent's false or vexatious claim or defence.
glossary.adjournment costs: Costs ordered under section 35B against a party who defaults on a required step or obtains an adjournment, to reimburse the other side's attendance expenses.
glossary.condition precedent: A requirement that must be satisfied before a party is entitled to take a further step, such as continuing to prosecute a suit or defence.
glossary.delay: Postponement in the progress of a suit, which section 35B specifically targets by shifting the cost of the resulting wasted attendance.
glossary.execution of orders: The rule that orders of a court, not just decrees, may also be enforced through the machinery of execution provided in the Code, so far as the nature of the order permits.
glossary.Court of first instance: The trial court that originally heard and decided the suit, as distinct from any appellate court that later reviewed its decision.
glossary.appellate jurisdiction: The power of a higher court to review and revise the decisions of a subordinate court on appeal.
glossary.jurisdictional transfer: The shifting of a case or proceeding from one court to another that has been vested with the requisite jurisdiction to handle it.
glossary.executing Court: The court that actually carries out (executes) a decree, which may or may not be the same court that originally passed it.
glossary.Court which passed the decree: Includes not only the original trial court but, where that court's jurisdiction has ceased or been transferred, the court which would now have jurisdiction to try the suit afresh.
glossary.transfer of decree: The formal act by which a court that passed a decree sends it to another competent court for execution, typically because the judgment-debtor or their property lies outside the first court's local limits.
glossary.sufficient property: Property of the judgment-debtor within the local limits of the transferring court's jurisdiction that is adequate to satisfy the decree, the absence of which is a ground for transferring the decree elsewhere.
glossary.suo motu transfer: A transfer of a decree for execution that a court initiates on its own motion, without a formal application by the decree-holder.
glossary.interstate transfer of decree: The procedure for sending a decree passed by a court in one State to a court in another State for execution, subject to prescribed conditions and rules.
glossary.prescribed rules: The procedural rules framed under the Code (typically in the First Schedule or by rule-making authority) that govern how a particular step, such as an inter-State transfer, must be carried out.
glossary.certificate of execution: A formal certification sent by the executing court back to the court which passed (or transferred) the decree, stating the manner in which the decree has been executed or the extent to which execution has failed.
glossary.failure of execution: The outcome where a decree, or part of it, remains unsatisfied despite execution proceedings, which must be certified to the court that passed or transferred the decree.
glossary.transferred decree: A decree that has been sent by the court which passed it to another court for the purpose of execution.
glossary.same powers: The principle that a court executing a transferred decree has, in relation to that execution, the same powers as if it had itself passed the decree.
glossary.disobedience: The judgment-debtor's or a third party's refusal or failure to comply with a decree or an order of the court, which may attract coercive consequences such as attachment or detention.
glossary.obstruction: Conduct by the judgment-debtor or another person that hinders or resists the executing court's officers in carrying out execution, punishable in the same manner as disobedience.
glossary.onward transfer: The further sending of an already-transferred decree from the court currently holding it to yet another court for execution.
glossary.non-Code-territory decree: A decree passed by a Civil or Revenue Court in a part of India to which the Code of Civil Procedure does not extend, which nonetheless may be executed under the Code's provisions once transferred.
glossary.extraterritorial execution: The execution of a decree in territory beyond the local limits of the court that originally passed it, achieved through the mechanism of transfer to a court having jurisdiction over that territory.
glossary.Revenue Court decree: A decree or order passed by a Revenue Court, which the Code permits to be executed as if it were a decree of a Civil Court, subject to any special rules governing Revenue Courts.
glossary.notification: An official government notification, published in the Official Gazette, that may extend or apply particular provisions of the Code to a specified territory or class of case.
glossary.reciprocating territory: Any country or territory outside India notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette as a reciprocating territory, whose superior courts' decrees can be executed in India as if passed by an Indian District Court.
glossary.superior Courts: In the context of reciprocating territory, the courts specified in the Central Government's notification as the courts of that territory whose decrees qualify for direct execution in India under Section 44A.
glossary.money decree: A decree for the payment of a sum of money, as distinguished from a decree for other reliefs such as possession or injunction; only money decrees (with certain exclusions) from reciprocating territories are directly executable under Section 44A.
glossary.arbitration award: A decision rendered by an arbitrator or arbitral tribunal; sums payable under an award are excluded from the definition of a Section 44A money decree even if the award has been (or could be) enforced as a decree in the original territory.
glossary.execution outside India: The enforcement of an Indian decree through a court situated outside India, permitted under Section 45 only where the State Government has specifically notified that court for this purpose.
glossary.notified Court: A court formally declared, by Government notification in the Official Gazette, to be one to which a particular statutory provision applies.
glossary.precept: A direction issued by the court which passed a decree to another competent court, instructing it to attach specified property of the judgment-debtor as an urgent, temporary measure pending fuller execution proceedings.
glossary.attachment under precept: The temporary attachment of a judgment-debtor's property carried out by a court acting on a precept, which lapses after two months unless extended or converted into a full transfer-based attachment.
glossary.separate suit bar: The rule under Section 47 that disputes between decree-holder and judgment-debtor about the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree must be resolved by the executing court itself, not through an independent fresh suit.
glossary.representative of a party: A person who stands in the shoes of an original party to the suit for execution purposes, such as a legal heir, assignee, or other successor-in-interest.
glossary.auction-purchaser as party: The legal fiction under Explanation II to Section 47 treating the buyer at a court-ordered execution sale as a party to the original suit, so that possession disputes involving them fall within the executing court's jurisdiction.
glossary.repealed section: A section of an Act that has been formally omitted or withdrawn by a later enactment, and no longer has legal effect, though its number may be retained in the text for continuity.
glossary.limitation for execution: The statutory time-limit within which a decree-holder must apply to execute a decree, currently twelve years from the date the decree becomes enforceable under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
glossary.transferee of a decree: A person to whom a decree has been assigned or transferred by the original decree-holder, who then becomes entitled to execute it.
glossary.equities against original decree-holder: Fair defences, set-offs, or claims that a judgment-debtor could have raised against the original decree-holder, and which remain available even after the decree is transferred to someone else.
glossary.legal representative liability: The principle that a deceased judgment-debtor's legal representative is liable to satisfy the decree only out of estate property that has come into their hands and has not been duly disposed of, not out of their own personal assets.
glossary.duly disposed of: Estate property that a legal representative has properly and legitimately spent, distributed, or applied (for example toward the deceased's genuine debts), and which is therefore no longer available to satisfy a decree.
glossary.modes of execution: The range of methods by which a court may enforce a decree under Section 51 — delivery of specific property, attachment and sale, arrest and detention, appointment of a receiver, or any other manner suited to the relief granted.
glossary.arrest and detention safeguard: The proviso to Section 51 restricting imprisonment for a money decree to cases where the court, after a show-cause hearing, records written reasons finding bad-faith evasion, proven refusal to pay despite means, or a fiduciary breach.
glossary.fiduciary capacity: A position of trust in which a person is legally bound to account for money or property held on another's behalf, such as a trustee, agent, or guardian.
glossary.show-cause opportunity: The mandatory hearing a judgment-debtor must be given before being committed to prison in execution of a money decree, allowing them to explain why detention should not be ordered.
glossary.decree against legal representative: A decree passed directly against a person in their capacity as the legal representative of a deceased person, ordering payment out of the deceased's estate property.
glossary.failure to account for estate property: A legal representative's inability to satisfy the court that estate property which came into their possession was properly applied, which can expose them to execution as if the decree were personal, up to the unaccounted value.
glossary.ancestral property liability: The extension, via Section 53, of Sections 50 and 52's execution rules to ancestral property in the hands of a son or descendant that is liable under Hindu law for a deceased ancestor's debt.
glossary.pious obligation: The Hindu law doctrine under which a son or descendant may be liable to pay off an ancestor's debts out of ancestral property, on grounds of religious and moral duty, independent of personal liability.
glossary.revenue estate partition: The division of an undivided landed estate that is assessed to Government land revenue, carried out under Section 54 by revenue authorities rather than the civil court itself.
glossary.Collector's role in partition: The statutory function assigned to the Collector (or a gazetted subordinate deputed by the Collector) to execute a civil court's decree for partition or separate possession of a share of a revenue-assessed estate.
glossary.dwelling-house entry safeguards: The set of procedural protections in Section 55 restricting when and how an officer may enter a dwelling-house to arrest a judgment-debtor, including a night-time entry ban and special notice to women observing purdah.
glossary.insolvency discharge route: The option given to a judgment-debtor arrested for a money decree to apply to be declared insolvent, potentially leading to discharge from detention if no bad faith is shown and insolvency law requirements are met.
glossary.security for insolvency application: A guarantee furnished by an arrested judgment-debtor, to the court's satisfaction, that they will apply for insolvency within one month and appear as required, which can secure their release from arrest in the meantime.
glossary.absolute bar on arresting women for mone: The non-obstante rule in Section 56 that flatly forbids a court from ordering the arrest or civil-prison detention of a woman to execute a decree for payment of money.
glossary.subsistence allowance: The monthly maintenance amount, fixed by the State Government on scales that may vary by rank, race, and nationality, payable for the upkeep of a judgment-debtor detained in civil prison.
glossary.maximum detention period: The statutory cap under Section 58 on how long a judgment-debtor may be kept in civil prison for a money decree, tiered according to the size of the decretal amount.
glossary.monetary threshold for detention: The minimum decretal amount below which Section 58(1A) forbids any order of civil-prison detention against a judgment-debtor for a money decree.
glossary.release without discharge of debt: The principle that a judgment-debtor's release from civil prison on expiry of the permitted detention period does not extinguish the underlying debt, though it does bar re-arrest under the same decree.
glossary.release on medical grounds: The set of powers under Section 59 permitting cancellation of an arrest warrant, or release from arrest or civil-prison detention, on account of a judgment-debtor's serious illness or, in the case of already-committed persons, infectious or contagious disease.
glossary.warrant cancellation for illness: The court's power under Section 59(1) to cancel an arrest warrant issued against a judgment-debtor before it is executed, on the ground of the judgment-debtor's serious illness.
glossary.attachable property: The broad category of a judgment-debtor's movable and immovable saleable property, and property over which they hold a beneficial disposing power, that is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree under Section 60(1).
glossary.exemption from attachment: The list of specific property categories under the proviso to Section 60(1) — such as basic necessities, tools of trade, certain wages and pensions, and insurance proceeds — that are protected from attachment or sale in execution of a decree.
glossary.attachable salary portion: The fraction of a judgment-debtor's monthly salary that may be attached in execution — generally the first exempt slice plus one-third of the remainder attachable (two-thirds exempt) for ordinary decrees, with a larger attachable share for maintenance decrees.
glossary.waiver of exemption void: The rule under Section 60(1A) that any agreement by which a person purports to give up in advance the benefit of an attachment exemption is legally void and unenforceable.
glossary.future maintenance right: A person's right to receive maintenance payments in the future, which under Section 60(1)(n) cannot be attached or sold in execution of a decree because it has not yet accrued as property.
glossary.agricultural produce exemption order: A general or special order that a State Government may publish in the Official Gazette under Section 61, exempting a specified portion of agricultural produce from attachment so that a farmer judgment-debtor can continue cultivation and support their family until the next harvest.
glossary.seizure of movable property safeguards: The procedural protections under Section 62 governing how and when an officer executing process may enter a dwelling-house to seize movable property, including a night-time entry ban and special protection for women in purdah, mirroring the arrest safeguards in Section 55.
glossary.multiple-attachment priority rule: The rule under Section 63 determining which of several courts that have attached the same property under different decrees gets to receive and realize that property and decide related claims — the highest-grade court, or, if equal in grade, whichever attached first.
glossary.Court of highest grade: Among courts that have attached the same property under different decrees, the court occupying the superior position in the judicial hierarchy, which under Section 63 takes priority in receiving and realizing that property.
glossary.private alienation void: The rule under Section 64 that any private transfer, delivery, or contrary payment concerning attached property made after attachment is void as against claims enforceable under that attachment.
glossary.pre-attachment registered contract excep: The exception under Section 64(2) preserving a private transfer of attached property from being voided, where the transfer was made pursuant to a contract both entered into and registered before the attachment took place.
glossary.retroactive vesting of title: The principle under Section 65 that a purchaser's ownership of immovable property bought at an execution sale is deemed to date back to the time of the sale itself, once the sale becomes absolute, rather than to the later confirmation date.
glossary.sale becoming absolute: The point at which an execution sale of property is confirmed under the applicable procedural rules (typically after the period for filing objections has passed without success), after which the purchaser's title is treated as vesting from the original sale date.
glossary.uncertain land interest sale rules: Special rules a State Government may frame by Gazette notification under Section 67 to govern the sale, in execution of money decrees, of land interests too uncertain or undetermined in value for ordinary sale procedure.
glossary.rateable distribution of assets: The proportionate division, under Section 73, of assets recovered from a judgment-debtor among all decree-holders who had applied for execution of their money decrees against that debtor before the assets were received by the court.
glossary.mortgagee surplus exclusion: The rule under Section 73's proviso (a) that a mortgagee or incumbrancer whose secured property is sold in execution is not entitled to share in any surplus proceeds beyond satisfying their own secured interest.
glossary.incumbrance sale proceeds order: The statutory order of priority under Section 73's proviso (c) for applying proceeds from the sale of immovable property sold to discharge an incumbrance: sale expenses first, then the decree amount, then subsequent incumbrances, and finally rateable distribution among other applicant decree-holders.
glossary.resistance to possession: Obstruction by a judgment-debtor, or someone acting on their behalf, that prevents a decree-holder or execution-sale purchaser from actually obtaining possession of immovable property they are legally entitled to.
glossary.detention for obstruction of possession: The coercive remedy under Section 74 allowing a court to detain a judgment-debtor or other obstructing person in civil prison for up to thirty days where they have, without just cause, resisted a decree-holder or purchaser from obtaining possession of immovable property.
glossary.commission (court): A formal delegation by a court to a court-appointed commissioner to carry out a specified task — such as examining a witness, investigating a site, auditing accounts, or effecting a partition — under Section 75 and Order XXVI.
glossary.local investigation commission: A commission issued under Section 75(b) directing a commissioner to visit and investigate a place or site relevant to the suit, and report findings back to the court.
glossary.ministerial act commission: A commission issued under Section 75(g) delegating a routine, non-adjudicatory administrative task to a court-appointed commissioner.

sections.title: Short title, commencement and extent
sections.raw_text:
1. (1) This Act may be cited as the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
(2) It shall come into force on the first day of January, 1909.
(3) It extends to the whole of India except—
(a) [***]
(b) the State of Nagaland and the tribal areas:
Provided that the State Government concerned may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the provisions of this Code or any of them to the whole or part of the State of Nagaland or such tribal areas, as the case may be, with such supplemental, incidental or consequential modifications, as may be specified in the notification.
Explanation.—In this clause, "tribal areas" means the territories which immediately before the 21st day of January, 1972, were included in the tribal areas of Assam, as referred to in paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.
(4) In the absence of any specific provision to the contrary, nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any special jurisdiction or power conferred, or any special form of procedure prescribed, by or under any other law for the time being in force.

breakdown.plain_summary: The opening section names the Act, fixes its commencement date as 1 January 1909, and marks out its territorial reach. The Code applies across India except Nagaland and the Sixth Schedule tribal areas of Assam (as they stood in 1972), though the State Government can switch it on there by gazette notification with local modifications. Sub-section (4) is a residual savings clause: unless the Code expressly says otherwise, it does not override special jurisdiction or procedure created by other laws.
essential_elements: Sub-section (2) fixes 1 January 1909 as the date the Code came into force.
Sub-section (3) extends the Code to the whole of India except Nagaland and the tribal areas defined by reference to the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.
The proviso lets the State Government extend the Code (wholly or partly, with modifications) to Nagaland or the tribal areas by Gazette notification.
Sub-section (4) preserves special jurisdiction, powers, or procedures created by other laws unless the Code expressly overrides them.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a general default-applicability clause, not a code of exhaustive procedure — special statutes (e.g., the Provincial/Presidency Small Cause Courts Acts, the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, tribunal statutes) can and do displace the Code's ordinary procedure for their own proceedings.

The Nagaland/tribal-area exclusion is a live, checkable jurisdictional fact — before invoking the Code in those areas, confirm whether a State notification has actually extended the relevant provisions.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the Code's on/off switch and geographic map, not as substantive law. When a procedural question arises in Nagaland or an excluded tribal area, the first move is to check for an extending notification under the proviso, not to assume the Code applies by default.

sections.title: Definitions

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 2 is the Code's dictionary, and by far its most-cited provision for setting up other doctrines — especially the decree/order distinction, which controls appeal rights throughout the Code. A decree is a conclusive adjudication on rights in controversy (preliminary, final, or partly both); an order is any other formal decision of a civil Court. Other defined terms (decree-holder, judgment-debtor, legal representative, mesne profits, pleader, public officer) recur across execution, representation, and evidentiary provisions.
essential_elements: Clause (2): a decree conclusively determines rights in controversy in the suit; it excludes appealable orders and default dismissals, but expressly includes rejection of a plaint and section 144 restitution determinations.

The Explanation to clause (2) distinguishes preliminary decrees (more proceedings needed to fully dispose of the suit) from final decrees (suit fully disposed of), and allows a decree to be partly each.
Clause (12) defines mesne profits as actual or ordinary-diligence-obtainable profits from wrongful possession, plus interest, excluding the wrongful possessor's own improvement-driven profits.
Clause (11) gives "legal representative" a wide meaning covering not just heirs but intermeddlers with a deceased person's estate and successors-in-representative-capacity.
Clause (17) enumerates eight categories of "public officer" (a)-(h), relevant to service-of-notice, evidentiary, and immunity provisions elsewhere in the Code.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The decree/order line is not merely academic — misclassifying an adjudication determines whether an appeal lies as of right (decree) or only as an order under section 104/Order XLIII, or not at all.

Clause (7B)'s definition of "India" excluding Jammu and Kashmir reflects the historical position under Article 370-era special status; practitioners should check current constitutional and statutory position given J&K's post-2019 reorganisation, since Code provisions referencing this clause may need updated reading.
"Order" under clause (14) is defined only negatively (not a decree) — its content is filled in by Order XLIII Rule 1, which lists which orders are appealable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Keep this section open as a running reference while reading the rest of the Code — nearly every substantive provision leans on one of these definitions, and the decree/order distinction in particular should be tested against clause (2) every time an appeal-eligibility question comes up.

sections.title: Subordination of Courts
sections.raw_text: 3. For the purposes of this Code, the District Court is subordinate to the High Court, and every Civil Court of a grade inferior to that of a District Court and every Court of Small Causes is subordinate to the High Court and District Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section fixes the hierarchical chain of civil courts for the Code's purposes: the District Court answers to the High Court, and every court below District Court grade — including Small Cause Courts — answers to both the District Court and the High Court.
essential_elements: The District Court is subordinate to the High Court.
Every Civil Court of a grade inferior to the District Court, and every Court of Small Causes, is subordinate to both the High Court and the District Court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This hierarchy underpins revisional jurisdiction (section 115), appellate jurisdiction, and the transfer powers in sections 22-25 — subordination as defined here is a precondition for those powers to operate.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section to quickly answer 'who can this court's orders be revised or appealed to' — it is the structural map that sections 24, 25, and 115 build on.

sections.title: Savings
sections.raw_text:
4. (1) In the absence of any specific provision to the contrary, nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any special or local law now in force or any special jurisdiction or power conferred, or any special form of procedure prescribed, by or under any other law for the time being in force.
(2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the proposition contained in sub-section (1), nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any remedy which a landholder or landlord may have under any law for the time being in force for the recovery of rent of agricultural land from the produce of such land.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 4 confirms the Code's default, non-overriding character. Unless the Code specifically says otherwise, it does not cut down special or local laws, or special jurisdiction/procedure created elsewhere, and it specifically preserves a landlord's separate remedies for recovering agricultural rent from produce.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) is a general savings clause protecting special/local laws and special jurisdiction or procedure, absent an express contrary provision in the Code.
Sub-section (2) specifically preserves landlord/landholder remedies for recovering agricultural rent out of the land's produce.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This overlaps with section 1(4) — both function as anti-override clauses; section 4 is broader (special/local laws generally) while section 1(4) is framed around special jurisdiction/procedure.
breakdown.how_to_read: Invoke this section whenever a special statute (rent law, revenue law, tribunal statute) appears to conflict with the Code's general procedure — the Code yields unless it expressly overrides.

sections.title: Application of the Code to Revenue Courts
sections.raw_text:
5. (1) Where any Revenue Courts are governed by the provisions of this Code in those matters of procedure upon which any special enactment applicable to them is silent, the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that any portions of those provisions which are not expressly made applicable by this Code shall not apply to those Courts, or shall only apply to them with such modifications as the State Government may prescribe.
(2) "Revenue Court" in sub-section (1) means a Court having jurisdiction under any local law to entertain suits or other proceedings relating to the rent, revenue or profits of land used for agricultural purposes, but does not include a Civil Court having original jurisdiction under this Code to try such suits or proceedings as being suits or proceedings of a civil nature.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets a State Government dial down how much of the Code applies to Revenue Courts — courts that handle agricultural rent/revenue/profit disputes under local land-revenue law — where their own special enactment is silent on a procedural point.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) empowers the State Government to notify that Code provisions not expressly made applicable shall not apply, or apply only with modification, to Revenue Courts.

Sub-section (2) defines "Revenue Court" as a court with local-law jurisdiction over agricultural rent/revenue/profit disputes, expressly excluding ordinary Civil Courts exercising civil-nature jurisdiction over the same subject matter.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Whether the Code applies to a given Revenue Court proceeding, and to what extent, is not fixed by the Code alone — it depends on the applicable State notification and the Revenue Court's own special enactment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Before applying general Code procedure to a Revenue Court matter, check the special enactment and any State notification under this section — the Code may only be a gap-filler there, not the primary source of procedure.

sections.title: Pecuniary jurisdiction
sections.raw_text: 6. Save in so far as is otherwise expressly provided, nothing herein contained shall operate to give any Court jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject-matter of which exceeds the pecuniary limits (if any) of its ordinary jurisdiction.

breakdown.plain_summary: A court cannot try a suit whose subject-matter value exceeds its own pecuniary jurisdiction limit, unless the Code expressly says otherwise somewhere else.
essential_elements: The default rule bars a court from entertaining suits above its pecuniary jurisdiction ceiling.
This default yields only where the Code itself expressly provides otherwise.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Pecuniary jurisdiction limits themselves are fixed by State-specific Civil Courts Acts, not by this Code — section 6 only states the general principle that such limits bind the court.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this alongside the applicable State Civil Courts Act to check valuation-based jurisdiction at the plaint-drafting stage — an over-valued or under-valued suit risks return/rejection under Order VII.

sections.title: Provincial Small Cause Courts

breakdown.plain_summary: Small Cause Courts (constituted under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, or exercising similar jurisdiction) run on their own simplified procedure — this section carves out large swathes of the Code, including suits excluded from small-cause cognizance, execution against immovable property, and specific Chapters/Sections, as inapplicable to them.
essential_elements: The carve-out excludes Code provisions on suits excepted from small-cause cognizance and on executing decrees in such suits, including execution against immovable property.
It expressly excludes sections 9, 91, 92 and Chapters IX, X and XI from applying to Small Cause Courts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a procedural simplification device, not a substantive jurisdiction grant — the Small Cause Courts Act itself defines what these courts can hear; this section just narrows which Code machinery governs how they hear it.
breakdown.how_to_read: When a matter is before a Provincial Small Cause Court, check this list first — assuming the full Code applies (e.g., trying to invoke Chapter IX-XI machinery) will misfire.

sections.title: Presidency Small Cause Courts
sections.raw_text:
8. Save as provided in this section and in sections 24, 38 to 41, 75, clauses (a), (b) and (c), 76, 77, 157 and 158, none of the provisions of this Code, other than sections 27, 32 and 33, sections 96 to 112 and sections 115, 116 and 152 shall extend to any suit or proceeding in any Court of Small Causes established at Calcutta, Madras or Bombay:
Provided that the High Courts of Judicature at Fort William, Madras and Bombay respectively may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare all or any of the provisions of this Code not hereby extended to those Courts, and not inconsistent with the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, to be applicable to the said Courts or with the aforesaid Act, respectively, or to any class of suits therein, and may, in like manner, from time to time, withdraw any such declaration:
Provided also that all such declarations and withdrawals of declarations shall be subject to the previous sanction of the State Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Presidency towns' Small Cause Courts (Calcutta, Madras, Bombay) get an even narrower default slice of the Code than the provincial ones — only a short specified list of sections applies by default — but the respective High Courts can extend further Code provisions to them by gazette notification, subject to State Government sanction.
essential_elements: By default, only the specifically listed sections/provisions (including 24, 27, 32-33, 38-41, 75(a)-(c), 76-77, 96-112, 115-116, 152, 157-158) extend to these Courts.
The first proviso lets the relevant High Court extend additional, not-inconsistent Code provisions to these Courts by Official Gazette notification, and later withdraw such extension.
The second proviso conditions any such High Court declaration or withdrawal on prior State Government sanction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Any extension is also capped by consistency with the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 — the High Court cannot extend a Code provision that conflicts with that Act.
breakdown.how_to_read: For litigation in a Presidency Small Cause Court, verify both this section's default list and whether the relevant High Court has issued an extending notification — do not assume ordinary Code procedure applies wholesale.

sections.title: Courts to try all civil suits unless barred
sections.raw_text:
9. The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred.
Explanation I.—A suit in which the right to property or to an office is contested is a suit of a civil nature, notwithstanding that such right may depend entirely on the decision of questions as to religious rites or ceremonies.
Explanation II.—For the purposes of this section, it is immaterial whether or not any fees are attached to the office referred to in Explanation I or whether or not such office is attached to a particular place.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Code's foundational jurisdiction-conferring section: civil courts have default jurisdiction over every suit of a civil nature, unless a statute expressly or impliedly bars that particular kind of suit. Even disputes over religious offices or property turning on religious-rite questions remain civil in nature, and it does not matter whether the office carries fees or is tied to a specific place.
essential_elements: The default rule is broad, positive jurisdiction: all suits of a civil nature are triable, subject only to express or implied bars.
An express bar is a statute specifically ousting civil court jurisdiction over a class of disputes (e.g., committing them exclusively to a tribunal).
An implied bar arises where a special statute's scheme (a self-contained code of rights and remedies) necessarily excludes the ordinary civil court's jurisdiction, even without express words.
Explanation I confirms property/office disputes remain civil in nature even if they turn on religious-rite questions.
Explanation II clarifies fee-attachment or place-attachment of the office is irrelevant to that classification.
exceptions_and_qualifications: "Civil nature" is broader than "civil proceeding" — the test looks to whether the right claimed and relief sought are civil, not to the character of the parties or the forum in which the dispute arose.

Implied ouster is construed strictly against exclusion of civil court jurisdiction — courts presume jurisdiction survives unless the special statute's language and scheme clearly show otherwise, especially where the special forum cannot grant the relief sought or where the special provision itself is under challenge as ultra vires.
breakdown.how_to_read: When a defendant argues the civil court lacks jurisdiction, locate the specific statutory bar (express or implied) rather than arguing in the abstract — section 9's default is jurisdiction, and the burden is on the party asserting the bar to point to the ousting provision or scheme.

sections.title: Stay of suit
sections.raw_text:
10. No Court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title where such suit is pending in the same or any other Court in India having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed, or in any Court beyond the limits of India established or continued by the Central Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court.
Explanation.—The pendency of a suit in a foreign Court does not preclude the Courts in India from trying a suit founded on the same cause of action.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 10 prevents parallel civil litigation on the same issue: once a suit raising a matter directly and substantially in issue has already been filed between the same parties (or their privies claiming under the same title), a later suit on that same matter cannot be tried while the earlier one is pending, whether the earlier suit is in an Indian court, a comparable court abroad established by the Central Government, or the Supreme Court.
essential_elements: The bar applies only where the matter in issue is directly and substantially the same in both suits, not merely similar or overlapping.
The parties (or persons claiming under the same title as them) must be the same in both suits.
The earlier suit must be pending and in a court competent to grant the relief claimed in it.
The rule is a stay/trial-bar, not a bar to institution — the later suit can be filed, just not tried, until the earlier one is decided.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation clarifies that a foreign-court suit's pendency does not by itself stop Indian courts from trying a suit on the same cause of action — the stay mechanism under this section operates only among courts of the described kind (Indian courts, Central-Government-established courts abroad with like jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court).
breakdown.how_to_read: Check this section at the earliest stage when a client's proposed suit might overlap with pending litigation — raising it early (via an application to stay) avoids wasted trial proceedings and conflicting decrees on the same issue.

sections.title: Res judicata
sections.raw_text:
11. No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court.
Explanation I.—The expression "former suit" shall denote a suit which has been decided prior to the suit in question whether or not it was instituted prior thereto.
Explanation II.—For the purposes of this section, the competence of a Court shall be determined irrespective of any provisions as to a right of appeal from the decision of such Court.
Explanation III.—The matter above referred to must in the former suit have been alleged by one party and either denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other.
Explanation IV.—Any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in such former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit.
Explanation V.—Any relief claimed in the plaint, which is not expressly granted by the decree, shall for the purposes of this section, be deemed to have been refused.
Explanation VI.—Where persons litigate bona fide in respect of public right or of a private right claimed in common for themselves and others, all persons interested in such right shall, for the purposes of this section, be deemed to claim under the persons so litigating.
Explanation VII.—The provisions of this section shall apply to a proceeding for the execution of a decree and references in this section to any suit, issue or former suit shall be construed as references, respectively, to a proceeding for the execution of the decree, question arising in such proceeding and a former proceeding for the execution of that decree.
Explanation VIII.—An issue heard and finally decided by a Court of limited jurisdiction, competent to decide such issue, shall operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit, notwithstanding that such Court of limited jurisdiction was not competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised.
key_terms: matter directly and substantially in issue

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 11 is the Code's res judicata bar: once a matter directly and substantially in issue has actually been heard and finally decided between the same parties (or privies) by a competent court, it cannot be re-litigated in a later suit or issue. Eight Explanations flesh out edge cases — from which suit counts as "former" (Explanation I), to constructive res judicata for matters that ought to have been raised (Explanation IV), to representative-litigation binding effect (Explanation VI), to extension into execution proceedings (Explanation VII) and limited-jurisdiction court decisions (Explanation VIII).
essential_elements: The bar requires the same matter directly and substantially in issue in both the former and the present suit/issue.
The parties (or those claiming under them, under the same title) must be identical across both proceedings.

The former suit must have been decided by a court competent to try the subsequent suit, and the issue must have been heard and finally decided (Explanation II disregards mere appeal-right differences for this competence test).
Explanation I: "former suit" means whichever suit was decided first, regardless of filing order.
Explanation IV (constructive res judicata): matters that ought to have been raised as attack or defence in the former suit are deemed to have been in issue, even if never actually pleaded.
Explanation VI extends res judicata to bind all persons interested in a bona fide public or common private right litigated by representative parties.
Explanation VII extends the whole section to execution proceedings.
Explanation VIII (inserted 1976) makes a limited-jurisdiction court's decision on an issue operate as res judicata even where that court could not have tried the later, larger suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Res judicata requires an actual hearing and final decision on the merits of the matter — it does not apply to matters left undecided, or decided only on a technical/procedural ground without touching the merits, except as extended by the Explanations.
Explanation V treats an unaddressed relief claimed in the plaint but not expressly granted as impliedly refused, which itself becomes res judicata against re-claiming it later.

Constructive res judicata (Explanation IV) is a frequently litigated trap for parties who split their claims or defences across successive suits — failing to raise an available ground the first time can permanently bar it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Plead res judicata as a mixed question of fact and law, supported by the pleadings, issues, and judgment of the former suit — courts look at the substance of what was actually in controversy and decided, not just matching case titles. When defending against it, check whether the earlier decision was truly "heard and finally decided" on that specific matter, or whether the forum was actually incompetent to decide it.

sections.title: Bar to further suit
sections.raw_text: 12. Where a plaintiff is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action, he shall not be entitled to institute a suit in respect of such cause of action in any Court to which this Code applies.

breakdown.plain_summary: If procedural rules (elsewhere in the Code, notably Order II Rule 2 on splitting claims) already bar a plaintiff from bringing a further suit on a given cause of action, section 12 makes that bar absolute across every court to which the Code applies — the plaintiff cannot route around it by suing in a different court.
essential_elements: The bar operates only where some rule of the Code already precludes a further suit on the cause of action in question.
Once that rule-based preclusion exists, it extends to bar suit in any Code-governed court, not just the court where the original suit was brought.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section is a reinforcing/jurisdiction-wide extension provision — the substantive preclusion itself typically arises from Order II Rule 2 (omission to sue for whole claim or relief) rather than from section 12 in isolation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this together with Order II Rule 2 when assessing whether a client's proposed second suit on a related cause of action is viable — the preclusion, once triggered, cannot be escaped by forum-shopping to another court.

sections.title: When foreign judgment not conclusive

breakdown.plain_summary: A foreign judgment generally binds the same parties on matters it directly adjudicated — but section 13 carves out six situations (a)-(f) where an Indian court will refuse to treat it as conclusive: lack of jurisdiction, no decision on the merits, a flawed view of international law or refusal to recognise Indian law, breach of natural justice, fraud, or upholding a claim that breaches Indian law.
essential_elements: The general rule is conclusiveness of a foreign judgment on matters it directly adjudicated, between the same parties or privies under the same title.
Exception (a): the foreign court must have had competent jurisdiction by international-law/private-international-law standards, not merely its own domestic law.
Exception (b): the judgment must be on the merits, not a default or purely procedural dismissal.
Exception (c): an incorrect view of international law, or refusal to apply Indian law where applicable, defeats conclusiveness.
Exception (d): proceedings opposed to natural justice (e.g., no proper notice or opportunity to be heard) defeat conclusiveness.
Exception (e): a judgment obtained by fraud (on the court or on the party) is not conclusive.
Exception (f): a judgment sustaining a claim founded on breach of Indian law is not conclusive.
exceptions_and_qualifications: These six exceptions are exhaustive grounds of attack when resisting enforcement or reliance on a foreign judgment — a party challenging conclusiveness must bring the case within one of clauses (a)-(f), not merely disagree with the foreign court's outcome.
breakdown.how_to_read: When a foreign judgment is sought to be relied upon (including via section 14's presumption), test it methodically against each of the six exceptions in turn — this is the standard checklist used to resist recognition or execution.

sections.title: Presumption as to foreign judgments
sections.raw_text: 14. The Court shall presume, upon the production of any document purporting to be a certified copy of a foreign judgment, that such judgment was pronounced by a Court of competent jurisdiction, unless the contrary appears on the record; but such presumption may be displaced by proving want of jurisdiction.

breakdown.plain_summary: Producing a certified copy of a foreign judgment triggers a rebuttable presumption that it was pronounced by a competent court — the opposing party bears the burden of proving want of jurisdiction to displace that presumption.
essential_elements: The presumption is triggered by production of a document purporting to be a certified copy of the foreign judgment.
The presumption is that the judgment was pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction.
The presumption is rebuttable — it falls away if the contrary appears on the record, or if want of jurisdiction is affirmatively proved.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a burden-shifting evidentiary rule, not a conclusive validation — it works alongside, not instead of, the section 13(a) competent-jurisdiction exception.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use a certified copy to establish the initial presumption efficiently, but be ready to meet a jurisdiction challenge with independent proof of how the foreign court's jurisdiction was founded, since the presumption yields once want of jurisdiction is shown.

sections.title: Court in which suits to be instituted
sections.raw_text: 15. Every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it.

breakdown.plain_summary: A plaintiff must file suit in the lowest-grade court that is competent (has jurisdiction) to try it — not in a higher court merely for convenience or perceived advantage.
essential_elements: The obligation is to sue in the lowest grade of court that has jurisdiction over the suit's subject-matter and value.
"Competent" here refers to the court's pecuniary and subject-matter jurisdiction to try the suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is chiefly an administrative/docket-management rule to prevent overburdening higher courts; a suit instituted in a higher court in breach of this section is not automatically a nullity, but the objection can be raised and is governed by the section 21 framework on jurisdictional objections.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check the applicable court-fee/pecuniary jurisdiction schedule at the drafting stage to identify the correct lowest-grade court — filing too high invites an avoidable objection and possible transfer.

sections.title: Suits to be instituted where subject-matter situate
sections.raw_text:
16. Subject to the pecuniary or other limitations prescribed by any law, suits—
(a) for the recovery of immovable property with or without rent or profits,
(b) for the partition of immovable property,
(c) for foreclosure, sale or redemption in the case of a mortgage of or charge upon immovable property,
(d) for the determination of any other right to or interest in immovable property,
(e) for compensation for wrong to immovable property,
(f) for the recovery of movable property actually under distraint or attachment,
shall be instituted in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate:
Provided that a suit to obtain relief respecting, or compensation for wrong to, immovable property held by or on behalf of the defendant, may where the relief sought can be entirely obtained through his personal obedience, be instituted either in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate, or in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the defendant actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain.
Explanation.—In this section "property" means property situate in India.

breakdown.plain_summary: For suits about immovable property (recovery, partition, mortgage foreclosure/sale/redemption, other rights/interests, compensation for wrong to it) or movable property already under distraint/attachment, venue is normally fixed by where the property is situated. A proviso softens this for relief that can be fully satisfied through the defendant's personal obedience (e.g., specific performance-type relief) — such suits can instead be filed where the defendant resides, does business, or works for gain.
essential_elements: Clauses (a)-(f) list the categories of suits governed by this situs-based venue rule.
The default venue is the court within whose local limits the immovable property is situate.

The proviso creates an alternative venue — the defendant's residence/business/work-for-gain location — but only where the relief sought is one satisfiable entirely through the defendant's personal obedience.
The Explanation confines "property" under this section to property situate in India.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso's personal-obedience alternative is narrow — it applies only when the decree can be wholly executed by compelling the defendant's personal act, not where the relief inherently requires action on/against the property itself (e.g., a sale or partition decree operating on the property).
breakdown.how_to_read: Classify the suit's true relief carefully before choosing venue: property-situs suits generally must go where the property sits, and the personal-obedience proviso is the narrow exception, not the rule — misjudging this risks a return of plaint for want of jurisdiction.

sections.title: Suits for immovable property situate within jurisdiction of different Courts
sections.raw_text:
17. Where a suit is to obtain relief respecting, or compensation for wrong to, immovable property situate within the jurisdiction of different Courts, the suit may be instituted in any Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction any portion of the property is situate:
Provided that, in respect of the value of the subject-matter of the suit, the entire claim is cognizable by such Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: When immovable property forming the subject of a suit straddles the territorial jurisdiction of more than one court, the plaintiff can sue in any one of those courts within whose limits any part of the property lies — provided that court's pecuniary jurisdiction is large enough to cognize the entire claim's value.
essential_elements: The rule applies where the property in suit spans multiple courts' local jurisdictional limits.
The plaintiff may choose any one such court, so long as some portion of the property lies within its local limits.
The proviso requires that the chosen court's pecuniary jurisdiction be sufficient to cover the full value of the subject-matter claimed.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a venue-convenience provision for property straddling boundaries; it does not dispense with the ordinary pecuniary jurisdiction requirement under section 6.
breakdown.how_to_read: When property spans two or more districts, pick the forum strategically among the qualifying courts, but always cross-check pecuniary competence for the full claim value against the proviso before filing.

sections.title: Place of institution where local limits of jurisdiction uncertain
sections.raw_text:
18. (1) Where it is alleged to be uncertain within the local limits of the jurisdiction of which of two or more Courts any immovable property is situate, any one of those Courts may, if satisfied that there is such uncertainty, record a statement to that effect and thereupon proceed to entertain and dispose of any suit relating to that property, and its decree in the suit shall have the same effect as if the property were situate within the local limits of its jurisdiction:
Provided that the suit is one with respect to which the Court is competent as regards the nature and value of the suit to exercise jurisdiction.
(2) Where a statement has not been recorded under sub-section (1), and an objection is taken before an Appellate or Revisional Court that a decree or order in a suit relating to such property was made by a Court not having jurisdiction where the property is situate, the Appellate or Revisional Court shall not allow the objection unless in its opinion there was, at the time of the institution of the suit, no reasonable ground for uncertainty as to the Court having jurisdiction with respect thereto and there has been a consequent failure of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: When it is genuinely uncertain which of two or more courts has territorial jurisdiction over immovable property, any one of those courts can record that uncertainty and then proceed with the suit as if the property were within its jurisdiction — as long as it is otherwise competent by nature and value. If this recording step is skipped, an appellate/revisional court will still not disturb the decree on this ground unless there was no reasonable ground for the uncertainty at the time of filing and a failure of justice actually resulted.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) lets any one of the genuinely competing courts record its satisfaction of uncertainty and then validly try the suit as though the property were within its limits.
That court must still otherwise be competent as to the nature and value of the suit.

Sub-section (2) protects decrees even where no formal statement of uncertainty was recorded — an appellate/revisional court will only entertain a jurisdiction objection if there was no reasonable ground for uncertainty AND a failure of justice resulted.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a curative/validating provision aimed at preventing decrees from being upset on hyper-technical local-limits disputes; it does not cure genuine, non-borderline lack of jurisdiction.
breakdown.how_to_read: Where property location straddles an unclear boundary, proactively get the uncertainty recorded under sub-section (1) at the outset — relying on sub-section (2)'s protective shield later is a fallback, not a substitute, since it requires proving both unreasonableness of any ground for certainty and actual failure of justice.

sections.title: Suits for compensation for wrongs to person or movables
sections.raw_text:
19. Where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within the local limits of the jurisdiction of one Court and the defendant resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of another Court, the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts.
Illustrations
(a) A, residing in Delhi, beats B in Calcutta. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi.
(b) A, residing in Delhi, publishes in Calcutta statements defamatory of B. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi.

breakdown.plain_summary: For tort-type suits (personal injury or wrongs to movable property), the plaintiff gets a choice of venue where the place of the wrong and the defendant's residence/business fall in different courts' jurisdictions — either the place-of-wrong court or the defendant's-location court.
essential_elements: The suit must be for compensation for a wrong done to the person or to movable property.
The rule applies specifically when the wrong-location and the defendant's residence/business/work-for-gain location fall under different courts.
The plaintiff has the option to sue in either court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is narrower than section 20's general venue rule — it is specific to person/movable-property wrong suits, and only kicks in when the two relevant locations diverge across court jurisdictions.
breakdown.how_to_read: When advising a tort plaintiff, compare both potential venues for practical advantages (e.g., evidence location, convenience) since the choice is entirely the plaintiff's under this section.

sections.title: Other suits to be instituted where defendants reside or cause of action arises
sections.raw_text:
20. Subject to the limitations aforesaid, every suit shall be instituted in a Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction—
(a) the defendant, or each of the defendants where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain; or
(b) any of the defendants, where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, provided that in such case either the leave of the Court is given, or the defendants who do not reside, or carry on business, or personally work for gain, as aforesaid, acquiesce in such institution; or
(c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises.
Explanation.—A corporation shall be deemed to carry on business at its sole or principal office in India or, in respect of any cause of action arising at any place where it has also a subordinate office, at such place.
Illustrations
(a) A is a tradesman in Calcutta, B carries on business in Delhi. B, by his agent in Calcutta, buys goods of A and requests A to deliver them to the East India Railway Company. A delivers the goods accordingly in Calcutta. A may sue B for the price of the goods either in Calcutta, where the cause of action arose, or in Delhi, where B carries on business.
(b) A resides at Simla, B at Calcutta and C at Delhi. A, B and C being together at Benaras, C makes a promissory note payable on demand and delivers it to B, who at Benaras sues A and C on the note. The suit may be brought in any Court in which any one of the defendants might be sued, but if the leave of the Court is not given, it must be brought where A and C actually and voluntarily reside, carry on business or personally work for gain, since A and C do not both reside, carry on business or personally work for gain at Benaras.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Code's residual, general venue provision, applying whenever no more specific rule (sections 16-19) governs: a suit can be filed where the (sole) defendant resides/does business/works for gain, or where any one of multiple defendants does so (with leave of court or acquiescence of the others), or where the cause of action wholly or partly arises.
essential_elements: Clause (a) covers the single-defendant (or all-defendants-together) residence/business/work location.
Clause (b) covers multiple defendants at different locations — suit can be at any one defendant's location, but only with either court leave or the other defendants' acquiescence.
Clause (c) covers the cause-of-action location, whether the whole or only part of the cause of action arose there.
The Explanation deems a corporation to carry on business at its sole/principal office in India, or at a subordinate office for a cause of action arising there.
