exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (b)'s leave-or-acquiescence requirement is a real procedural gate — suing a non-local defendant purely by joining them with a local co-defendant, without leave or acquiescence, is vulnerable to a jurisdiction objection under section 21.

"Cause of action" under clause (c) means the bundle of facts that must be proved to obtain the relief claimed — partial arising is sufficient, so long as some material fact forming part of the cause of action arose within the forum.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the default venue toolbox for most ordinary suits (contract, debt, etc.) — work through clauses (a)-(c) in order, and for multi-defendant suits always check whether leave or acquiescence is actually in place before relying on a non-local defendant's presence to found jurisdiction.

sections.title: Objections to jurisdiction
sections.raw_text:
21. (1) No objection as to the place of suing shall be allowed by any Appellate or Revisional Court unless such objection was taken in the Court of first instance at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.
(2) No objection as to the competence of a Court with reference to the pecuniary limits of its jurisdiction shall be allowed by any Appellate or Revisional Court unless such objection was taken in the Court of first instance at the earliest possible opportunity, and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.
(3) No objection as to the competence of the executing Court with reference to the local limits of its jurisdiction shall be allowed by any Appellate or Revisional Court unless such objection was taken in the executing Court at the earliest possible opportunity, and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 21 protects decrees from being upset on jurisdictional technicalities raised too late. Objections to place of suing, pecuniary jurisdiction, or (for executing courts) local territorial limits are all barred on appeal or revision unless raised at the earliest possible opportunity in the court of first instance (or executing court) AND the objecting party shows a consequent failure of justice.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) governs place-of-suing objections; sub-section (2) (inserted 1976) governs pecuniary-jurisdiction objections; sub-section (3) (inserted 1976) governs local-limits objections to the executing court's competence.
All three require the objection to have been raised at the earliest possible opportunity — generally by or at the settlement of issues — in the trial or executing court.
All three additionally require proof of a consequent failure of justice before an appellate or revisional court will entertain the objection.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a twin-condition test — timeliness alone is not enough, and failure of justice alone (raised too late) is not enough; both must be satisfied together.

This section addresses procedural/territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction defects, which are curable/waivable in this manner — it does not validate a decree passed wholly without subject-matter jurisdiction, which remains a nullity regardless of when objected to.
breakdown.how_to_read: Raise any place-of-suing, pecuniary-jurisdiction, or executing-court-local-limits objection immediately, at or before the settlement of issues — waiting until appeal is a common, often-fatal drafting/strategy trap given the strict two-part test in this section.

sections.title: Bar on suit to set aside decree on objection as to place of suing
sections.raw_text:
21A. No suit shall lie to set aside a decree passed in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, on any ground based on an objection as to the place of suing.
Explanation.—The expression "former suit" means a suit which has been decided prior to the decision in the suit in which the objection as to the place of suing is raised.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section (inserted in 1976) closes an indirect route around section 21's timing bar: a party cannot file a fresh, separate suit to set aside an earlier decree purely on the ground that the earlier suit was filed in the wrong place.
essential_elements: The bar applies to a fresh suit whose object is to set aside a decree passed in a former suit between the same parties or their privies under the same title.
The ground barred is specifically an objection as to place of suing (territorial venue), not other jurisdictional or merits-based grounds.
The Explanation defines "former suit" as whichever suit was decided earlier in time.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This provision only bars place-of-suing-based collateral attacks; it does not immunise a decree from challenge on genuine want of subject-matter/pecuniary jurisdiction or other independent grounds available under general law.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a client wants to challenge an old decree, check first whether the sole ground is territorial venue — if so, section 21A forecloses a fresh suit, and the correct remedy (if any) had to be pursued as an objection under section 21 in the original proceeding itself.

sections.title: Power to transfer suits which may be instituted in more than one Court
sections.raw_text: 22. Where a suit may be instituted in any one of two or more Courts and is instituted in one of such Courts, any defendant, after notice to the other parties, may, at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, apply to have the suit transferred to another Court, and the Court to which such application is made, after considering the objections of the other parties (if any), shall determine in which of the several Courts having jurisdiction the suit shall proceed.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a suit could validly have been filed in more than one competent court, a defendant may apply, at the earliest opportunity and after notifying the other parties, to have it transferred to one of the other eligible courts; the receiving court then decides, after hearing objections, which of the eligible courts should actually proceed with it.
essential_elements: The provision applies only when the suit could properly have been instituted in more than one court.
The application must come from a defendant, with notice to other parties, at the earliest possible opportunity (generally at or before settlement of issues).
The court to which the application is made decides, after considering objections, which of the several eligible courts should proceed with the suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is distinct from section 21's objection-to-jurisdiction mechanism — section 22 presumes the suit was validly filed in a competent court and is about choosing among multiple equally valid venues, not challenging validity.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this provision (rather than section 21) when the objection is not that the filing court lacked jurisdiction, but that a different, equally competent court would be more appropriate — and raise it promptly, since it carries the same earliest-opportunity discipline as section 21.

sections.title: To what Court application lies
sections.raw_text:
23. (1) Where the several Courts having jurisdiction are subordinate to the same Appellate Court, the application under section 22 shall be made to the Appellate Court.
(2) Where such Courts are subordinate to different Appellate Courts but to the same High Court, the application shall be made to the said High Court.
(3) Where such Courts are subordinate to different High Courts, the application shall be made to the High Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the Court in which the suit is brought is situate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section routes a section 22 transfer application to the correct forum, scaled to how far apart the competing courts sit in the judicial hierarchy: same Appellate Court's subordinates go to that Appellate Court; different Appellate Courts under the same High Court go to that High Court; and courts under different High Courts go to the High Court local to the court where the suit was actually filed.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): common Appellate Court scenario — application goes to that Appellate Court.
Sub-section (2): different Appellate Courts but common High Court — application goes to that High Court.
Sub-section (3): different High Courts entirely — application goes to the High Court local to where the suit was instituted.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a simple routing table for section 22 applications — identify the lowest common judicial authority over the competing courts and file there.

sections.title: General power of transfer and withdrawal
sections.raw_text:
24. (1) On the application of any of the parties and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desired to be heard, or of its own motion without such notice, the High Court or the District Court may at any stage—
(a) transfer any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same, or
(b) withdraw any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to it, and—
(i) try or dispose of the same, or
(ii) transfer the same for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same, or
(iii) retransfer the same for trial or disposal to the Court from which it was withdrawn.
(2) Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.
(3) For the purposes of this section,—
(a) Courts of Additional and Assistant Judges shall be deemed to be subordinate to the District Court;
(b) "proceeding" includes a proceeding for the execution of a decree or order.
(4) The Court trying any suit transferred or withdrawn under this section from a Court of Small Causes shall, for the purposes of such suit, be deemed to be a Court of Small Causes.
(5) A suit or proceeding may be transferred under this section from a Court which has no jurisdiction to try it.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the broad, general transfer/withdrawal power of the High Court and District Court over any suit, appeal, or proceeding pending in or under them, exercisable at any stage, on application or on their own motion, with the receiving court free to either retry the matter or continue from where it was left off.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1)(a) permits transfer from the High Court/District Court itself down to a competent subordinate court.

Sub-section (1)(b) permits withdrawal of a matter from a subordinate court, followed by the withdrawing court trying it itself, transferring it onward to another competent subordinate court, or sending it back to the original court.
Sub-section (2) lets the receiving court choose to retry from scratch or continue from the transfer/withdrawal point, subject to any special directions.
Sub-section (3)(a) deems Additional and Assistant Judge courts subordinate to the District Court for this section; (3)(b) extends "proceeding" to execution proceedings.
Sub-section (4) preserves Small Cause Court character/procedure for a suit transferred from such a court.
Sub-section (5) (inserted 1976) clarifies transfer power extends even to a matter pending in a court that lacked jurisdiction to try it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power can be exercised suo motu, without any party's application, distinguishing it from the narrower, party-driven section 22 mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Reach for section 24 (rather than section 22) whenever the goal is a discretionary administrative transfer for convenience, docket management, or to cure a jurisdictional defect — it is the High Court/District Court's general supervisory transfer tool, broader than section 22's multiple-competent-venue scenario.

sections.title: Power of Supreme Court to transfer suits, etc.
sections.raw_text:
25. (1) On the application of a party, and after notice to the other party and after hearing him, the Supreme Court may, at any stage, if satisfied that an order under this section is expedient for the ends of justice, direct that any suit, appeal or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other Civil Court in one State to a High Court or other Civil Court in any other State.
(2) Every application under this section shall be made by a motion which shall be supported by an affidavit.
(3) The Court to which such suit, appeal or other proceeding is transferred shall, subject to any special directions in the order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred to it.
(4) In dismissing any application under this section, the Supreme Court may, if it is of opinion that the application was frivolous or vexatious, order the applicant to pay by way of compensation to any person who has opposed the application such sum, not exceeding two thousand rupees, as it considers appropriate in the circumstances of the case.
(5) The law applicable to any suit, appeal or other proceeding transferred under this section shall be the law which the Court in which the suit, appeal or other proceeding was originally instituted ought to have applied to such suit, appeal or proceeding.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Supreme Court holds the ultimate, inter-State transfer power — it can move a suit, appeal, or proceeding from a High Court or civil court in one State to one in another, on a party's application (by motion with supporting affidavit, after notice and hearing) wherever expedient for the ends of justice, with a costs deterrent against frivolous or vexatious applications.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) empowers transfer at any stage, on the expediency-for-ends-of-justice standard, only after notice to and hearing of the other party.
Sub-section (2) requires the application to be by motion supported by affidavit.
Sub-section (3) lets the transferee court retry or continue from the transfer point, subject to special directions in the transfer order.
Sub-section (4) lets the Supreme Court penalise a frivolous or vexatious application with compensation up to ₹2,000 payable to the party who opposed it.
Sub-section (5) preserves the choice of law — the transferred matter continues to be governed by the law the originating court ought to have applied, not the transferee State's law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is reserved for genuinely inter-State transfers; intra-State transfers between courts under the same High Court are handled under sections 22-24, not this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: Reserve section 25 applications for real inter-State transfer needs (e.g., witness safety, fair trial concerns, convenience spanning States) and expect the Supreme Court to scrutinise expediency carefully given the express frivolous-application cost deterrent in sub-section (4).

sections.title: Institution of suits
sections.raw_text:
26. (1) Every suit shall be instituted by the presentation of a plaint or in such other manner as may be prescribed.
(2) In every plaint, facts shall be proved by affidavit.

breakdown.plain_summary: A civil suit formally begins when a plaint is presented (or through whatever other manner is prescribed by rules), and the facts pleaded in it must be supported by affidavit.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) fixes presentation of a plaint (or a prescribed alternative manner) as the mode of instituting a suit.
Sub-section (2) (inserted 2002) requires the facts in every plaint to be proved by affidavit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The affidavit requirement in sub-section (2) works alongside Order VI Rule 15A, which prescribes the form and manner of that affidavit.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat plaint presentation as the trigger date for limitation and other institution-linked consequences, and ensure the accompanying affidavit is in the prescribed form — an incomplete or missing affidavit is a common, easily avoidable filing defect.

sections.title: Summons to defendants
sections.raw_text: 27. Where a suit has been duly instituted, a summons may be issued to the defendant to appear and answer the claim and may be served in manner prescribed on such day not beyond thirty days from date of the institution of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a suit is duly instituted, the court issues a summons calling the defendant to appear and answer the claim, to be served in the prescribed manner, returnable on a day within thirty days of institution.
essential_elements: A summons issues only after the suit has been duly instituted.
It must be served in the manner prescribed by the rules.
It must call for appearance on a day not beyond thirty days from the date of institution of the suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check the summons's return date against the thirty-day outer limit from institution when scrutinising procedural compliance, and pair this section with Order V's detailed service-of-summons machinery.

sections.title: Service of summons where defendant resides in another State
sections.raw_text:
28. (1) A summons may be sent for service in another State to such Court and in such manner as may be prescribed by rules in force in that State.
(2) The Court to which such summons is sent shall, upon receipt thereof, proceed as if it had been issued by such Court and shall then return the summons to the Court of issue together with the record (if any) of its proceedings with regard thereto.
(3) Where the language of the summons sent for service in another State is different from the language of the record referred to in sub-section (2), a translation of the record,—
(a) in Hindi, where the language of the Court issuing the summons is Hindi, or
(b) in Hindi or English where the language of such record is other than Hindi or English,
shall also be sent together with the record sent under that sub-section.

breakdown.plain_summary: For a defendant in another State, the issuing court routes the summons through the receiving State's own court and rules; the receiving court executes it as if it were its own summons and returns both the summons and its service record, with a Hindi/English translation attached if the languages differ.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): the summons is sent to a court in the other State, served under that State's own prescribed rules.
Sub-section (2): the receiving court treats it as its own summons, then returns the summons plus its service record to the issuing court.
Sub-section (3) (inserted 1976): a translation (Hindi, or Hindi/English) accompanies the returned record where the languages differ.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this as the inter-State service channel distinct from section 29's cross-border (outside-India) channel — the two sections should not be conflated.

sections.title: Service of foreign summonses
sections.raw_text:
29. Summonses and other processes issued by—
(a) any Civil or Revenue Court established in any part of India to which the provisions of this Code do not extend, or
(b) any Civil or Revenue Court established or continued by the authority of the Central Government outside India, or
(c) any other Civil or Revenue Court outside India to which the Central Government has, by notification in the Official Gazette, declared the provisions of this section to apply,
may be sent to the Courts in the territories to which this Code extends, and served as if they were summonses issued by such Courts.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section creates a reciprocal service channel: summonses from certain non-Code-governed Indian courts, Central-Government-established courts abroad, or notified foreign courts can be routed into Code territory and served there exactly as if they were locally issued summonses.
essential_elements: Clause (a) covers Civil/Revenue Courts within India but outside the Code's territorial extent.
Clause (b) covers Civil/Revenue Courts established or continued by the Central Government outside India.
Clause (c) covers other foreign Civil/Revenue Courts specifically notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette as covered by this section.
Once channeled in, such process is served in Code territory exactly as if it were a domestic summons.
breakdown.how_to_read: Confirm notification status under clause (c) before assuming a particular foreign court's process qualifies for this service route — absent notification, that specific foreign court's summonses fall outside this mechanism.

sections.title: Power to order discovery and the like

breakdown.plain_summary: The court has a broad, flexible power — usable on its own motion or a party's application, at any time — to manage pre-trial evidentiary matters: interrogatories, admissions, discovery/inspection/production/impounding of documents or objects, summoning witnesses or document-holders, and directing proof of facts by affidavit.
essential_elements: Clause (a) covers the full discovery toolkit: interrogatories, admissions, and discovery/inspection/production/impounding/return of documents or material objects.
Clause (b) covers summoning persons needed to give evidence or produce documents/objects.
Clause (c) covers ordering proof of any fact by affidavit.
The power is exercisable at any time, suo motu or on application, subject to prescribed conditions and limitations.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the general engine behind pre-trial procedural orders (interrogatories, discovery, inspection) — pair it with the detailed machinery in Order XI (discovery and inspection) and Order XVI (summoning witnesses) when drafting or opposing such applications.

sections.title: Summons to witness
sections.raw_text: 31. The provisions in sections 27, 28 and 29 shall apply to summonses to give evidence or to produce documents or other material objects.

breakdown.plain_summary: The same service rules that govern defendant-summonses (timing, inter-State routing, foreign-court reciprocity) also apply to summonses issued to witnesses to give evidence or produce documents/objects.
essential_elements: Sections 27 (issuance/timing), 28 (inter-State service), and 29 (foreign summonses) are all extended to witness summonses by this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: When serving a witness summons across State lines or from outside Code territory, apply the identical mechanics used for defendant summonses under sections 27-29.

sections.title: Penalty for default

breakdown.plain_summary: If a person summoned under section 30 (e.g., for discovery-related attendance) defaults, the court has coercive tools to compel compliance: arrest warrant, attachment and sale of property, a fine up to ₹5,000, or a security-for-appearance order backed by committal to civil prison on default.
essential_elements: The power applies to compelling attendance of a person summoned specifically under section 30.
Clause (a): arrest warrant.
Clause (b): attachment and sale of the defaulter's property.
Clause (c): a fine, capped at ₹5,000.
Clause (d): a security-for-appearance order, with civil imprisonment as the consequence of default on furnishing security.
breakdown.how_to_read: Reserve reliance on this section for genuine section 30 summons defaults — it is a targeted enforcement tool, not a general contempt power, and each of the four listed measures (a)-(d) is a distinct order the court must specifically make.

sections.title: Judgment and decree
sections.raw_text: 33. The Court, after the case has been heard, shall pronounce judgment, and on such judgment a decree shall follow.

breakdown.plain_summary: After the case has been heard, the court must pronounce judgment, and a decree follows from that judgment — the two-step sequence (judgment first, decree drawn up from it) that structures how a civil suit concludes.
essential_elements: Judgment is pronounced only after the case has been heard.
The decree is the formal expression that follows from, and gives effect to, the judgment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this as the anchor for the judgment/decree sequence — read alongside section 2(2) (decree definition), section 2(9) (judgment definition), and Order XX for the detailed procedure on pronouncement and drawing up of decrees.

sections.title: Interest
sections.raw_text:
34. (1) Where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money, the Court may, in the decree, order interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable to be paid on the principal sum adjudged, from the date of the suit to the date of the decree, in addition to any interest adjudged on such principal sum for any period prior to the institution of the suit, with further interest at such rate not exceeding six per cent. per annum as the Court deems reasonable on such principal sum, from the date of the decree to the date of payment, or to such earlier date as the Court thinks fit:
Provided that where the liability in relation to the sum so adjudged had arisen out of a commercial transaction, the rate of such further interest may exceed six per cent. per annum, but shall not exceed the contractual rate of interest or where there is no contractual rate, the rate at which moneys are lent or advanced by nationalised banks in relation to commercial transactions.
Explanation I.—In this sub-section, "nationalised bank" means a corresponding new bank as defined in the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970.
Explanation II.—For the purposes of this section, a transaction is a commercial transaction, if it is connected with the industry, trade or business of the party incurring the liability.
(2) Where such a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest on such principal sum from the date of the decree to the date of payment or other earlier date, the Court shall be deemed to have refused such interest, and a separate suit therefor shall not lie.

breakdown.plain_summary: For money decrees, section 34 lets the court award three distinct interest components: pre-suit interest (if otherwise adjudged), pendente-lite interest (date of suit to date of decree) at a court-determined reasonable rate, and post-decree interest (decree to payment) generally capped at 6% per annum — except for commercial transactions, where it can go up to the contractual rate or the nationalised-bank commercial lending rate. Silence on post-decree interest is deemed a refusal, foreclosing a separate suit for it.
essential_elements: The power applies only where, and to the extent, a decree is for payment of money.
The court sets its own reasonable rate for interest from the date of suit to the date of decree.
Post-decree interest (decree to payment) is capped at 6% per annum as the general rule.
The proviso lifts that cap for commercial-transaction liabilities, allowing up to the contractual rate, or (absent a contractual rate) the nationalised banks' commercial lending rate.
Explanation I defines "nationalised bank"; Explanation II defines "commercial transaction" as one connected with the liable party's industry, trade, or business.
Sub-section (2) deems silence on further interest as a refusal, barring a fresh suit to claim it separately.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 6% cap is a default ceiling, not an entitlement — the court retains discretion on whether to award post-decree interest at all, and at what rate up to the applicable cap.
breakdown.how_to_read: When drafting prayer clauses in money suits, specifically plead for pendente-lite and post-decree interest (and, for commercial transactions, the higher contractual/bank rate) — silence in the decree is treated as a deemed refusal under sub-section (2), and there is no second bite via a fresh suit.

sections.title: Costs
sections.raw_text:
35. (1) Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, and to the provisions of any law for the time being in force, the costs of an incident to all suits shall be in the discretion of the Court, and the Court shall have full power to determine by whom or out of what property and to what extent such costs are to be paid, and to give all necessary directions for the purposes aforesaid. The fact that the Court has no jurisdiction to try the suit shall be no bar to the exercise of such powers.
(2) Where the Court directs that any costs shall not follow the event, the Court shall state its reasons in writing.

breakdown.plain_summary: Costs of and incidental to a suit are in the court's discretion — it decides who pays, out of what property, and how much, and can exercise this power even if it turns out the court lacked jurisdiction to try the suit itself. If costs are not awarded to follow the usual rule (the losing party pays), the court must record written reasons.
essential_elements: The general default is "costs follow the event" — the unsuccessful party ordinarily pays, though this section frames it as discretionary rather than an absolute rule.
The court determines who pays, out of what property, and to what extent, with full power to give necessary directions.
Lack of jurisdiction to try the suit does not disable the court's power to make costs orders.
Sub-section (2) requires written reasons whenever the court departs from the usual costs-follow-the-event approach.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A separate, later-inserted version of section 35 (applicable specifically to commercial disputes of specified value, per the Commercial Courts Act regime) sets out a more detailed, structured costs framework — check whether the dispute qualifies as a commercial dispute before relying on the general section 35 alone.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always ask for costs specifically in the prayer, and if arguing against the costs-follow-the-event default, be ready for the court to record reasons under sub-section (2) — this reasoned-departure requirement is a useful check when costs orders appear to deviate from outcome without explanation.

sections.title: Compensatory costs in respect of false or vexatious claims or defences
sections.raw_text:
35A. (1) If in any suit or other proceedings including an execution proceeding but excluding an appeal or a revision any party objects to the claim or defence on the ground that the claim or defence or any part of it is, as against the objector, false or vexatious to the knowledge of the party by whom it has been put forward, and if thereafter, as against the objector, such claim or defence is disallowed, abandoned or withdrawn in whole or in part, the Court, if it so thinks fit, may, after recording its reasons for holding such claim or defence to be false or vexatious, make an order for the payment to the objector by the party by whom such claim or defence has been put forward, of costs by way of compensation.
(2) No Court shall make any such order for the payment of an amount exceeding three thousand rupees or exceeding the limits of its pecuniary jurisdiction, whichever amount is less:
Provided that where the pecuniary limits of the jurisdiction of any Court exercising the jurisdiction of a Court of Small Causes under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, or under a corresponding law in force in any part of India to which the said Act does not extend and not being a Court constituted under such Act or law, are less than two hundred and fifty rupees, the High Court may empower such Court to award as costs under this section any amount not exceeding two hundred and fifty rupees and not exceeding those limits by more than one hundred rupees:
Provided, further, that the High Court may limit the amount which any Court or class of Courts is empowered to award as costs under this section.
(3) No person against whom an order has been made under this section shall, by reason thereof, be exempted from any criminal liability in respect of any claim or defence made by him.
(4) The amount of any compensation awarded under this section in respect of a false or vexatious claim or defence shall be taken into account in any subsequent suit for damages or compensation in respect of such claim or defence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets a party who successfully objects to an opponent's knowingly false or vexatious claim/defence (which is then disallowed, abandoned, or withdrawn) recover compensatory costs, capped at ₹3,000 or the court's pecuniary jurisdiction limit, whichever is lower — with the court required to record reasons for the false/vexatious finding, and the award neither shielding the wrongdoer from criminal liability nor precluding it being set off against a later damages suit on the same claim/defence.
essential_elements: Applies to suits and other proceedings, including execution, but expressly excludes appeals and revisions.
Requires an objection by a party that the claim/defence (or part of it) is false or vexatious to the knowledge of the party asserting it.
Requires the claim/defence to then actually be disallowed, abandoned, or withdrawn (in whole or part) as against the objector.
The court must record reasons for holding the claim/defence false or vexatious before awarding compensatory costs.
Sub-section (2) caps the award at ₹3,000 or the court's own pecuniary jurisdiction limit, whichever is less, with special (lower) sub-limits for certain Small Cause Courts under the provisos.
Sub-section (3) preserves criminal liability notwithstanding the civil costs order.
Sub-section (4) requires this compensation to be set off against any later damages suit on the same claim/defence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a distinct, additional remedy from ordinary section 35 costs — it specifically targets knowing falsity/vexatiousness, not mere loss on the merits.
breakdown.how_to_read: Plead section 35A compensatory costs as a specific, reasoned application (not just a request folded into general costs) when a party has knowingly advanced a false or vexatious claim or defence — and remember the modest statutory cap, which limits its deterrent value compared to a full damages suit.

sections.title: Costs for causing delay
sections.raw_text:
35B. (1) If, on any date fixed for the hearing of a suit or for taking any step therein, a party to the suit—
(a) fails to take the step which he was required by or under this Code to take on that date, or
(b) obtains an adjournment for taking such step or for producing evidence or on any other ground,
the Court may, for reasons to be recorded, make an order requiring such party to pay to the other party such costs as would, in the opinion of the Court, be reasonably sufficient to reimburse the other party in respect of the expenses incurred by him in attending the Court on that date, and payment of such costs, on the date next following the date of such order, shall be a condition precedent to the further prosecution of—
(a) the suit by the plaintiff, where the plaintiff was ordered to pay such costs,
(b) the defence by the defendant, where the defendant was ordered to pay such costs.
Explanation.—Where separate defences have been raised by the defendant or groups of defendants, payment of such costs shall be a condition precedent to the further prosecution of the defence by such defendants or groups of defendants as have been ordered by the Court to pay such costs.
(2) The costs, ordered to be paid under sub-section (1), shall not, if paid, be included in the costs awarded in the decree passed in the suit; but, if such costs are not paid, a separate order shall be drawn up indicating the amount of such costs and the names and addresses of the persons by whom such costs are payable and the order so drawn up shall be executable against such persons.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 35B is a delay deterrent: if a party defaults on a required procedural step on a fixed hearing date, or obtains an adjournment, the court can order it to reimburse the other side's costs of attendance that day — and payment of those costs by the next date becomes a condition precedent to that party continuing to prosecute its suit or defence at all.
essential_elements: Triggered by either failing to take a required step on a fixed date, or obtaining an adjournment (for a step, evidence, or any other ground).
The court must record reasons before ordering costs.
The costs are pegged to reasonably reimbursing the other party's attendance expenses for that date.
Payment by the next following date is a condition precedent to further prosecution of the suit (if the plaintiff defaulted) or the defence (if the defendant defaulted).
The Explanation extends this defence-by-defence, where separate defendants/groups have raised separate defences.
Sub-section (2) keeps these costs separate from the final decree's costs award if paid, but makes them independently executable via a separate order if unpaid.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is procedural-delay costs, distinct from both section 35 (general costs) and section 35A (false/vexatious-claim compensatory costs) — all three can operate independently in the same suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: Track adjournment and default costs orders carefully as litigation counsel — under sub-section (1), unpaid section 35B costs can genuinely stall further prosecution of a claim or defence, making prompt payment a real, not merely nominal, procedural obligation.

sections.title: Application to orders
sections.raw_text: 36. The provisions of this Code relating to the execution of decrees (including provisions relating to payment under a decree) shall, so far as they are applicable, be deemed to apply to the execution of orders (including payment under an order).

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part II (Execution) by extending the whole execution machinery built for decrees to orders as well, wherever applicable — so a court order (not just a decree) can be enforced using the Code's execution provisions.
essential_elements: All Code provisions on execution of decrees, including payment under a decree, extend to execution of orders and payment under an order, so far as applicable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat every subsequent execution-related section in Part II as applying to orders too, unless the specific provision's language or context makes it decree-specific.

sections.title: Definition of Court which passed a decree
sections.raw_text:
37. The expression "Court which passed a decree," or words to that effect, shall, in relation to the execution of decrees, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, be deemed to include,—
(a) where the decree to be executed has been passed in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction, the Court of first instance, and
(b) where the Court of first instance has ceased to exist or to have jurisdiction to execute it, the Court which, if the suit wherein the decree was passed was instituted at the time of making the application for the execution of the decree, would have jurisdiction to try such suit.
Explanation.—The Court of first instance does not cease to have jurisdiction to execute a decree merely on the ground that after the institution of the suit wherein the decree was passed or after the passing of the decree, any area has been transferred from the jurisdiction of that Court to the jurisdiction of any other Court; but, in every such case, such other Court shall also have jurisdiction to execute the decree, if at the time of making the application for execution of the decree it would have jurisdiction to try the said suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section defines, for execution purposes, which court counts as the "Court which passed a decree" — extending the phrase to the trial court even when the decree was actually passed in appeal, and to whichever court would now have jurisdiction to try the original suit if the original trial court has since ceased to exist or lost jurisdiction, including due to territorial boundary changes.
essential_elements: Clause (a): for an appellate decree, the "Court which passed a decree" includes the Court of first instance.
Clause (b): if the Court of first instance has ceased to exist or lost jurisdiction, it includes whichever court would now have jurisdiction to try that suit.

The Explanation clarifies that mere territorial reallocation does not, by itself, strip the original Court of first instance of execution jurisdiction — the new court over that area also gains concurrent execution jurisdiction if it would now have jurisdiction to try the suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section to identify the correct executing court whenever the decree was passed in appeal, or the original trial court's identity/jurisdiction has changed since the decree was passed — a common practical issue in long-running execution proceedings.

sections.title: Court by which decree may be executed
sections.raw_text: 38. A decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it, or by the Court to which it is sent for execution.

breakdown.plain_summary: A decree-holder can execute a decree either in the court that originally passed it, or in another court to which the decree has been sent for execution.
essential_elements: The Court which passed the decree has execution jurisdiction over it.
A Court to which the decree has been sent for execution (per section 39) also has execution jurisdiction over it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the gateway provision to the transfer-of-decree machinery in section 39 — read them together to determine where execution can validly proceed.

sections.title: Transfer of decree
sections.raw_text:
39. (1) The Court which passed a decree may, on the application of the decree-holder, send it for execution to another Court of competent jurisdiction,—
(a) if the person against whom the decree is passed actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or
(b) if such person has not property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree sufficient to satisfy such decree and has property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or
(c) if the decree directs the sale or delivery of immovable property situate outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed it, or
(d) if the Court which passed the decree considers for any other reason, which it shall record in writing, that the decree should be executed by such other Court.
(2) The Court which passed a decree may of its own motion send it for execution to any subordinate Court of competent jurisdiction.
(3) For the purposes of this section, a Court shall be deemed to be a Court of competent jurisdiction if, at the time of making the application for the transfer of decree to it, such Court would have jurisdiction to try the suit in which such decree was passed.
(4) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to authorise the Court which passed a decree to execute such decree against any person or property outside the local limits of its jurisdiction.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets the decree-passing court send the decree to another competent court for execution — on the decree-holder's application (in four listed scenarios: judgment-debtor's residence/business elsewhere, insufficient local property, out-of-jurisdiction immovable property, or any other recorded reason), or on its own motion to a subordinate court — while making clear it cannot itself execute beyond its own local limits.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1)(a)-(c) list specific grounds: judgment-debtor's actual residence/business/work location, insufficiency of local property, and out-of-jurisdiction immovable property subject to the decree.
Sub-section (1)(d) is a residual ground allowing transfer for any other reason, provided the court records it in writing.
Sub-section (2) allows the court to transfer suo motu to a subordinate court of competent jurisdiction.
Sub-section (3) defines competent jurisdiction for transfer purposes by reference to whether the receiving court would have had jurisdiction to try the original suit.
Sub-section (4) confirms the passing court itself cannot execute against persons/property outside its own local limits — transfer is the mechanism for reaching them.
breakdown.how_to_read: When the judgment-debtor or their assets are outside the passing court's territorial reach, apply for transfer under this section promptly rather than attempting extraterritorial execution directly, which sub-section (4) forecloses.

sections.title: Transfer of decree to Court in another State
sections.raw_text: 40. Where a decree is sent for execution in another State, it shall be sent to such Court and executed in such manner as may be prescribed by rules in force in that State.

breakdown.plain_summary: For inter-State execution, the decree is routed to a court and executed according to whatever rules are in force in the receiving State — mirroring the section 28 approach for inter-State summons service.
essential_elements: The receiving State's own prescribed rules govern which court the decree goes to and how it is executed there.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check the destination State's specific procedural rules before sending a decree there for execution — the mechanics are not uniform but locally prescribed.

sections.title: Result of execution proceedings to be certified
sections.raw_text: 41. The Court to which a decree is sent for execution shall certify to the Court which passed it the fact of such execution, or where the former Court fails to execute the same the circumstances attending such failure.

breakdown.plain_summary: The executing court must report back to the originating court on what happened — whether the decree was successfully executed, or if not, the circumstances of the failure — closing the loop on any transferred execution.
essential_elements: A certifying obligation arises on the executing court once execution is attempted.
The certificate must state either the fact of successful execution, or the circumstances of failure.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use the absence or content of this certificate as a practical checkpoint when tracking a transferred execution's progress — it is the formal record of what the transferee court actually did.

sections.title: Powers of Court in executing transferred decree

breakdown.plain_summary: The transferee court steps fully into the shoes of the original court for executing a transferred decree — same powers, same punishment authority over disobedience/obstruction, same appeal rules — and can even onward-transfer, proceed against a deceased judgment-debtor's legal representative, or attach the decree itself, though it must report such further orders back and cannot execute at a decree-transferee's instance or grant firm-execution leave beyond specific categories.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) gives the transferee court full original-court-equivalent execution powers, punishment powers over disobedience/obstruction, and identical appeal rules.
Sub-section (2) expressly extends this to onward transfer (section 39), execution against a deceased judgment-debtor's legal representative (section 50), and ordering attachment of the decree itself.
Sub-section (3) requires reporting such orders back to the original passing court.

Sub-section (4) withholds two specific powers: executing at the instance of a decree-transferee, and (for firm decrees) granting leave to execute against persons beyond the specific categories in Order XXI Rule 50(1)(b)/(c).
breakdown.how_to_read: When acting for a party in a transferred-decree execution, confirm the transferee court's power under sub-section (2) for any onward step contemplated, and check the sub-section (4) carve-outs before assuming full original-court powers apply without limit.

sections.title: Execution of decrees passed by Civil Courts in places to which this Code does not extend
sections.raw_text: 43. Any decree passed by any Civil Court established in any part of India to which the provisions of this Code do not extend, or by any Court established or continued by the authority of the Central Government outside India, may, if it cannot be executed within the jurisdiction of the Court by which it was passed, be executed in the manner herein provided within the jurisdiction of any Court in the territories to which this Code extends.

breakdown.plain_summary: A decree from a Civil Court outside the Code's territorial reach (or from a Central-Government-established court abroad) can still be executed within Code territory, using the Code's own execution procedure, if it cannot be executed where it was originally passed.
essential_elements: The originating court must be either within India but outside the Code's extended territory, or a Central-Government-established court outside India.
The decree must be otherwise unexecutable within the originating court's own jurisdiction.
Execution then proceeds within Code territory following the Code's ordinary execution procedure.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with section 44 (Revenue Court decrees) and section 44A (reciprocating-territory decrees) as the trio of provisions bringing outside-Code-territory decrees into the ordinary Code execution machinery.

sections.title: Execution of decrees passed by Revenue Courts in places to which this Code does not extend
sections.raw_text: 44. The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that the decrees of any Revenue Court in any part of India to which the provisions of this Code do not extend, or any class of such decrees, may be executed in the State as if they had been passed by Courts in that State.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lets a State Government, by gazette notification, extend Code-based execution to decrees passed by Revenue Courts operating outside the Code's territorial reach, treating them as if locally passed for execution purposes.
essential_elements: The power belongs to the State Government, exercised by Official Gazette notification.
It covers decrees (or a declared class of decrees) of Revenue Courts in non-Code-extended parts of India.
Once notified, such decrees are executable in the State as if passed by that State's own courts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Confirm the existence of a specific State notification before assuming a Revenue Court decree from a non-Code territory can be executed locally under this section.

sections.title: Execution of decrees passed by Courts in reciprocating territory
sections.raw_text:
44A. (1) Where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in India as if it had been passed by the District Court.
(2) Together with the certified copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the extent, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted and such certificate shall, for the purposes of proceedings under this section, be conclusive proof of the extent of such satisfaction or adjustment.
(3) The provisions of section 47 shall as from the filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceedings of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13.
Explanation 1.—"Reciprocating territory" means any country or territory outside India which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a reciprocating territory for the purposes of this section; and "superior Courts", with reference to any such territory, means such Courts as may be specified in the said notification.
Explanation 2.—"Decree" with reference to a superior Court means any decree or judgment of such Court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty, but shall in no case include an arbitration award, even if such an award is enforceable as a decree or judgment.

breakdown.plain_summary: This creates a streamlined direct-execution route for money decrees from designated "reciprocating territories" abroad: filing a certified copy (with a satisfaction/adjustment certificate) in a District Court lets that decree be executed as if it were the District Court's own — subject to the same execution-questions regime under section 47 and to the section 13(a)-(f) foreign-judgment exceptions, which the court must apply to refuse execution where they are made out.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): filing a certified copy of a reciprocating-territory superior court's decree in a District Court makes it executable as if it were that District Court's own decree.
Sub-section (2): an accompanying satisfaction/adjustment certificate from the foreign court is conclusive proof on that specific point.

Sub-section (3): section 47 (execution-related questions determined by the executing court) applies from filing, and the District Court must refuse execution if any of the section 13(a)-(f) exceptions to foreign-judgment conclusiveness is made out.
Explanation 1 defines "reciprocating territory" and "superior Courts" by reference to Central Government notification.
Explanation 2 confines "decree" here to money decrees/judgments, excluding tax/penalty sums and excluding arbitration awards even if otherwise decree-enforceable.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a direct-execution shortcut available only for notified reciprocating territories and their notified superior courts — a foreign money decree from a non-notified country must instead be sued upon as a cause of action (using section 13's conclusiveness rules) rather than directly executed under this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: Before invoking section 44A, confirm both that the foreign country is a notified reciprocating territory and that the specific court is a notified "superior Court" — absent both, direct execution is unavailable and a fresh suit on the foreign judgment is the correct route.

sections.title: Execution of decrees outside India.
sections.raw_text: So much of the foregoing sections of this Part as empowers a Court to send a decree for execution to another Court shall be construed as empowering a Court in any State to send a decree for execution to any Court established by the authority of the Central Government outside India to which the State Government has by notification in the Official Gazette declared this section to apply.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 45 extends the ordinary transfer-of-decree machinery (Sections 39-44A) so that an Indian court can send a decree for execution to a court set up by the Central Government outside India, but only where the State Government has specifically notified that this section applies to that foreign court.
essential_elements: The receiving court must be one established by the authority of the Central Government outside India.
The State Government must have issued a notification in the Official Gazette declaring Section 45 applicable to that court.
Once notified, the same procedural machinery used for domestic inter-Court transfer of decrees applies.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Without the specific Gazette notification, a decree cannot simply be sent abroad for execution under this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow bridge provision — read it together with Sections 39-44A, which supply the actual transfer mechanics; Section 45 only extends their reach to specially notified courts outside India.

sections.title: Precepts.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Upon the application of the decree-holder the Court which passed the decree may, whenever it thinks fit, issue a precept to any other Court which would be competent to execute such decree to attach any property belonging to the judgment-debtor and specified in the precept.
(2) The Court to which a precept is sent shall proceed to attach the property in the manner prescribed in regard to the attachment of property in execution of a decree:
Provided that no attachment under a precept shall continue for more than two months unless the period of attachment is extended by an order of the Court which passed the decree or unless before the determination of such attachment the decree has been transferred to the Court by which the attachment has been made and the decree-holder has applied for an order for the sale of such property.

breakdown.plain_summary: A precept is an emergency direction: the court that passed the decree can ask another competent court to urgently attach a judgment-debtor's property there, to stop the debtor from spiriting it away, even before a formal transfer of the decree for execution has been completed.
essential_elements: Issued only on the decree-holder's application, at the discretion of the court which passed the decree.
Directs a court competent to execute the decree to attach specified property of the judgment-debtor.
The receiving court attaches the property using the ordinary procedure for attachment in execution.

The attachment automatically lapses after two months unless extended by the passing court, or unless the decree itself is transferred to the attaching court and a sale application is made before the two months run out.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A precept only permits attachment, not sale — sale requires either an extension or an actual transfer of the decree plus a sale application.
breakdown.how_to_read: Think of a precept as a holding measure: attach first, formally transfer (or extend) later. The two-month clock in the proviso is the key practical trap.

sections.title: Questions to be determined by the Court executing decree.
sections.raw_text:
(1) All questions arising between the parties to the suit in which the decree was passed, or their representatives, and relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree, shall be determined by the Court executing the decree and not by a separate suit.
(3) Where a question arises as to whether any person is or is not the representative of a party, such question shall, for the purposes of this section, be determined by the Court.
Explanation I.—For the purposes of this section, a plaintiff whose suit has been dismissed and a defendant against whom a suit has been dismissed are parties to the suit.
Explanation II.—(a) For the purposes of this section, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree shall be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree is passed; and
(b) all questions relating to the delivery of possession of such property to such purchaser or his representative shall be deemed to be questions relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 47 channels all disputes about executing, discharging, or satisfying a decree into the executing court itself — the losing party cannot file a fresh, separate suit to relitigate execution disputes. The two Explanations widen who counts as a 'party' for this purpose, including a plaintiff or defendant whose case was dismissed and an auction-purchaser at the execution sale.
essential_elements: The dispute must be between parties to the suit (or their representatives) and must relate to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of the decree.
Such questions must be decided by the executing court, not through a fresh separate suit.
Disputes over whether someone is a legal representative of a party are also decided by the executing court under this section.
An auction-purchaser at the execution sale is deemed a party, and disputes about delivering possession to them are treated as execution questions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar applies only to questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of the decree — questions outside this scope (e.g. a genuinely independent cause of action) may still require a separate suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the foundational bar-on-separate-suits provision for execution disputes — pair it with Order XXI (execution procedure) in practice; a plaint challenging execution matters instead of an execution application risks rejection for want of a fresh cause of action.

sections.title: [Execution barred in certain cases.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Limitation Act, 1963 (36 of 1963), section 28, with effect from 1 January 1964. This section formerly barred execution of a decree after the expiry of twelve years from the date the decree became enforceable, subject to certain exceptions. Limitation for execution of decrees is now governed by the Limitation Act, 1963 (see Article 136 of its Schedule, prescribing a twelve-year period from the date the decree becomes enforceable).

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 48 is no longer in force. It used to cap how long a decree-holder could wait before executing a decree, but Parliament moved this subject entirely into the Limitation Act, 1963, which now governs the time-limit for execution.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1964.
The subject matter (limitation for execution of decrees) migrated to the Limitation Act, 1963.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Not to be confused with a currently operative rule — any argument on limitation for execution today must be founded on the Limitation Act, 1963, not on this repealed section.
breakdown.how_to_read: A numbering placeholder only — retained so that surrounding section numbers (47, 49...) keep their historical position; the actual live law is in the Limitation Act, 1963, Article 136.

sections.title: Transferee.
sections.raw_text: Every transferee of a decree shall hold the same subject to the equities (if any) which the judgment-debtor might have enforced against the original decree-holder.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a decree is transferred (assigned) to someone else, that new holder does not get a cleaner claim than the original decree-holder had — any fair defences or set-offs the judgment-debtor could have raised against the original decree-holder remain available against the transferee too.
essential_elements: Applies to any transferee who acquires a decree by assignment or operation of law.
The transferee steps into the shoes of the original decree-holder, taking the decree subject to existing equities.
The judgment-debtor may raise against the transferee any equitable defence that was available against the original decree-holder.
breakdown.how_to_read: A basic assignment-law principle imported into execution practice — useful defensively for a judgment-debtor facing execution by someone other than the original decree-holder.

sections.title: Legal representative.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where a judgment-debtor dies before the decree has been fully satisfied, the holder of the decree may apply to the Court which passed it to execute the same against the legal representative of the deceased.
(2) Where the decree is executed against such legal representative, he shall be liable only to the extent of the property of the deceased which has come to his hands and has not been duly disposed of; and, for the purpose of ascertaining such liability, the Court executing the decree may, of its own motion or on the application of the decree-holder, compel such legal representative to produce such accounts as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a judgment-debtor dies before paying off the decree, the decree-holder can pursue the deceased's legal representative — but only to the extent of estate property that actually reached the representative's hands and hasn't already been properly spent or distributed.
essential_elements: The judgment-debtor must have died before the decree was fully satisfied.
The decree-holder applies to the court which passed the decree to execute against the legal representative.
Liability of the legal representative is capped at the value of estate property received and not duly disposed of.
The executing court may compel the legal representative to produce accounts to establish the extent of that property.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Personal assets of the legal representative are not at risk — liability is limited strictly to inherited estate property that has not been properly disposed of.
breakdown.how_to_read: Central to enforcing decrees after a judgment-debtor's death; read with Sections 52 and 53 for related rules on decrees against legal representatives and ancestral property.

sections.title: Powers of Court to enforce execution.
sections.raw_text:
Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, the Court may, on the application of the decree-holder, order execution of the decree—
(a) by delivery of any property specifically decreed;
(b) by attachment and sale or by the sale without attachment of any property;
(c) by arrest and detention in prison for such period not exceeding the period specified in section 58, where arrest and detention is permissible under that section;
(d) by appointing a receiver; or
(e) in such other manner as the nature of the relief granted may require:
Provided that, where the decree is for the payment of money, execution by detention in prison shall not be ordered unless, after giving the judgment-debtor an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be committed to prison, the Court, for reasons recorded in writing, is satisfied—
(a) that the judgment-debtor, with the object or effect of obstructing or delaying the execution of the decree,—
(i) is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, or
(ii) has, after the institution of the suit in which the decree was passed, dishonestly transferred, concealed, or removed any part of his property, or committed any other act of bad faith in relation to his property, or
(b) that the judgment-debtor has, or has had since the date of the decree, the means to pay the amount of the decree or some substantial part thereof and refuses or neglects or has refused or neglected to pay the same, or
(c) that the decree is for a sum for which the judgment-debtor was bound in a fiduciary capacity to account.
Explanation.—In the calculation of the means of the judgment-debtor for the purposes of clause (b), there shall be left out of account any property which, by or under any law or custom having the force of law for the time being in force, is exempt from attachment in execution of the decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 51 lists the toolbox of ways a court can enforce a decree: handing over decreed property, attaching and selling property, arrest and imprisonment, appointing a receiver, or any other manner suited to the relief granted. But for money decrees, imprisonment is deliberately made the last resort — it requires a specific show-cause hearing and a written finding that the debtor is dodging payment in bad faith, genuinely has the means but refuses to pay, or breached a fiduciary duty to account.
essential_elements: Execution modes: delivery of specific property, attachment-and-sale (or sale without attachment), arrest and detention, receiver appointment, or another fitting manner.
For money decrees, imprisonment requires the judgment-debtor first be given an opportunity to show cause.
The court must record written reasons finding bad-faith evasion, proven ability but refusal to pay, or fiduciary breach before ordering detention.
Property exempt from attachment by law or custom is excluded when assessing the judgment-debtor's 'means' to pay.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Arrest and detention for a money decree is never automatic — it is squarely conditioned on the proviso's safeguards, reflecting a policy against routine imprisonment for civil debt.
breakdown.how_to_read: The practitioner's execution menu — Section 51 supplies the 'what', while Order XXI supplies the 'how'; the proviso is the single most litigated safeguard against misuse of arrest in money-decree execution.

sections.title: Enforcement of decree against legal representative.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where a decree is passed against a party as the legal representative of a deceased person, and the decree is for the payment of money out of the property of the deceased, it may be executed by the attachment and sale of any such property.
(2) Where no such property remains in the possession of the judgment-debtor and he fails to satisfy the Court that he has duly applied such property of the deceased as is proved to have come into his possession, the decree may be executed against the judgment-debtor to the extent of the property in respect of which he has failed so to satisfy the Court in the same manner as if the decree had been against him personally.
key_terms: failure to account for estate property

breakdown.plain_summary: When a decree is already passed against someone specifically as the legal representative of a deceased person (for money payable from the deceased's estate), execution first targets estate property. If that property is gone and the representative cannot show it was properly applied, execution can proceed against the representative personally, but only to the extent of the unaccounted property.
essential_elements: Applies where the decree itself was passed against a person in their capacity as legal representative.
Primary mode of execution is attachment and sale of the deceased's property.

If such property is no longer available and the representative cannot prove it was duly applied, execution proceeds against the representative as if the decree were personal — capped at the unaccounted value.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish from Section 50: Section 50 covers a judgment-debtor who dies after the decree, requiring a fresh execution application against the representative; Section 52 covers a decree already passed against the representative as such.

sections.title: Liability of ancestral property.
sections.raw_text: For the purposes of section 50 and section 52, property in the hands of a son or other descendant which is liable under Hindu law for the payment of the debt of a deceased ancestor, in respect of which a decree has been passed, shall be deemed to be property of the deceased which has come to the hands of the son or other descendant as his legal representative.

breakdown.plain_summary: Under Hindu law, sons and descendants can be liable for a deceased ancestor's debts out of ancestral property (the 'pious obligation' doctrine). Section 53 plugs this into the execution framework by deeming such ancestral property to be property of the deceased in the descendant's hands, so Sections 50 and 52 apply to it directly.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to property liable under Hindu law for an ancestor's debt.
Such property, in the hands of a son or other descendant, is deemed to be the deceased's property received by them as legal representative.
This deeming fiction makes Sections 50 and 52 directly applicable to ancestral property execution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Limited to property that is actually liable under Hindu law's pious-obligation doctrine — not all ancestral property automatically qualifies.
breakdown.how_to_read: A bridge provision connecting personal-law liability (Hindu law pious obligation) with the Code's execution machinery — relevant in joint-family debt-recovery litigation.

sections.title: Partition of estate or separation of share.
sections.raw_text: Where the decree is for the partition of an undivided estate assessed to the payment of revenue to the Government, or for the separate possession of a share of such an estate, the partition of the estate or the separation of the share shall be made by the Collector or any gazetted subordinate of the Collector deputed by him in this behalf, in accordance with the law (if any) for the time being in force relating to the partition, or the separate possession of shares, of such estates.

breakdown.plain_summary: For land that is assessed to Government land revenue, a civil court decree for partition or separation of a share is not carried out by the civil court itself — it is handed over to the Collector (or their deputed subordinate) to implement, following the applicable revenue-partition law.
essential_elements: Applies only to an undivided estate assessed to the payment of revenue to the Government.
Covers both decrees for partition of the whole estate and decrees for separate possession of a share.
Execution of the partition/separation is carried out by the Collector or a gazetted subordinate deputed by the Collector, not by the civil court's own executing machinery.
The actual partition follows revenue law governing partition of such estates, where such law exists.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Some States have substituted their own procedure by State Amendment (for example, Karnataka routes this through the Court itself, assisted by a revenue officer as Commissioner, rather than the Collector).
breakdown.how_to_read: A jurisdiction-splitting provision — remember that execution of revenue-estate partition decrees moves out of the civil court's hands into revenue administration, subject to State-specific variations.

sections.title: Arrest and detention.
sections.raw_text:
(1) A judgment-debtor may be arrested in execution of a decree at any hour and on any day, and shall, as soon as practicable, be brought before the Court, and his detention may be in the civil prison of the district in which the Court ordering the detention is situate, or, where such civil prison does not afford suitable accommodation, in any other place which the State Government may appoint for the detention of persons ordered by the Courts of such district to be detained:
Provided, firstly, that, for the purpose of making an arrest under this section, no dwelling-house shall be entered after sunset and before sunrise:
Provided, secondly, that no outer door of a dwelling-house shall be broken open unless such dwelling-house is in the occupancy of the judgment-debtor and he refuses or in any way prevents access thereto, but when the officer authorized to make the arrest has duly gained access to any dwelling-house, he may break open the door of any room in which he has reason to believe the judgment-debtor is to be found:
Provided, thirdly, that, if the room is in the actual occupancy of a woman who is not the judgment-debtor and who according to the customs of the country does not appear in public, the officer authorized to make the arrest shall give notice to her that she is at liberty to withdraw, and, after allowing a reasonable time for her to withdraw and giving her reasonable facility for withdrawing, may enter the room for the purpose of making the arrest:
Provided, fourthly, that, where the decree in execution of which a judgment-debtor is arrested, is a decree for the payment of money and the judgment-debtor pays the amount of the decree and the costs of the arrest to the officer arresting him, such officer shall at once release him.
(2) The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that any person or class of persons whose arrest might be attended with danger or inconvenience to the public shall not be liable to arrest in execution of a decree otherwise than in accordance with such procedure as may be prescribed by the State Government in this behalf.
(3) Where a judgment-debtor is arrested in execution of a decree for the payment of money and brought before the Court, the Court shall inform him that he may apply to be declared an insolvent, and that he may be discharged if he has not committed any act of bad faith regarding the subject of the application and if he complies with the provisions of the law of insolvency for the time being in force.
(4) Where a judgment-debtor expresses his intention to apply to be declared an insolvent and furnishes security, to the satisfaction of the Court, that he will within one month so apply, and that he will appear, when called upon, in any proceeding upon the application or upon the decree in execution of which he was arrested, the Court may release him from arrest, and, if he fails so to apply and to appear, the Court may either direct the security to be realized or commit him to the civil prison in execution of the decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 55 lays down the mechanics and safeguards for physically arresting and detaining a judgment-debtor: when and how entry into a dwelling-house may be made, special protection for women observing purdah, immediate release on payment, State-notified immunity for classes of persons, and a built-in escape route via insolvency proceedings.
essential_elements: Arrest can happen at any hour/day, but dwelling-house entry is barred between sunset and sunrise.
Breaking open an outer door requires actual occupancy-based refusal of access by the judgment-debtor.
A woman in purdah occupying the room must be given notice and reasonable time to withdraw before entry.
Immediate release follows if the judgment-debtor pays the decretal amount and arrest costs on the spot.
The State Government can exempt specified persons/classes from ordinary arrest procedure via notification.
On arrest for a money decree, the court must inform the debtor of the option to apply for insolvency discharge.
Security for a promised insolvency application can substitute for continued detention for up to one month.
exceptions_and_qualifications: These protections apply specifically to arrest procedure; Section 56 separately bars arrest of women altogether for money decrees.
breakdown.how_to_read: A heavily proviso-laden section — practitioners should treat the four provisos as a checklist when challenging (or executing) an arrest warrant for procedural irregularity.

sections.title: Prohibition of arrest or detention of women in execution of decree for money.
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in this Part, the Court shall not order the arrest or detention in the civil prison of a woman in execution of a decree for the payment of money.
key_terms: absolute bar on arresting women for money decrees

breakdown.plain_summary: A blanket, non-obstante rule: no woman may ever be arrested or detained in civil prison to enforce a money decree against her, regardless of anything else in this Part of the Code.
essential_elements: Applies specifically and only to decrees for the payment of money.
The bar is absolute — the non-obstante clause overrides any contrary provision elsewhere in this Part.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Limited to money decrees; it does not by itself bar other coercive modes of execution (such as attachment and sale) against a woman judgment-debtor.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but absolute protective provision — always cite it directly (no balancing test required) if arrest of a woman is sought for a money decree.

sections.title: Subsistence-allowance.
sections.raw_text: The State Government may fix scales, graduated according to rank, race and nationality, of monthly allowances payable for the subsistence of judgment-debtors.
