breakdown.plain_summary: The State Government sets the monthly maintenance allowance payable to a judgment-debtor while they are detained in civil prison, with scales that can vary by rank, race, and nationality.
essential_elements: Power vested in the State Government to fix the allowance scales.
Scales may be graduated according to rank, race, and nationality.
breakdown.how_to_read: A largely administrative provision, mainly relevant to confirming that a detained judgment-debtor is entitled to State-fixed subsistence, not left destitute in custody.

sections.title: Detention and release.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every person detained in the civil prison in execution of a decree shall be so detained,—
(a) where the decree is for the payment of a sum of money exceeding five thousand rupees, for a period not exceeding three months, and,
(b) where the decree is for the payment of a sum of money exceeding two thousand rupees, but not exceeding five thousand rupees, for a period not exceeding six weeks.
(1A) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that no order for detention of the judgment-debtor in civil prison in execution of a decree for the payment of money shall be made, where the total amount of the decree does not exceed two thousand rupees.
(2) A judgment-debtor released from detention under this section shall not merely by reason of his release be discharged from his debt, but he shall not be liable to be re-arrested under the decree in execution of which he was detained in the civil prison.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 58 caps how long a judgment-debtor can be kept in civil prison based on the size of the money decree, sets a minimum decree amount below which detention cannot be ordered at all, and clarifies that release from prison does not wipe out the underlying debt — it only bars re-arrest under that same decree.
essential_elements: Detention periods are tiered by decree amount: up to three months for decrees exceeding five thousand rupees; up to six weeks for decrees between two thousand and five thousand rupees.
No detention at all may be ordered where the total decretal amount does not exceed two thousand rupees.
Release on expiry of the permitted period does not discharge the debt itself.
Once released under this section, the judgment-debtor cannot be re-arrested under the same decree.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The monetary thresholds are the statutory figures as amended; they function as a floor below which imprisonment is barred outright, reflecting the same restrictive policy on civil imprisonment for debt seen in Section 51's proviso.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read with Section 51(c)'s cross-reference — the 'period specified in section 58' capping detention length. The core practitioner point: release under Section 58 is procedural, not a discharge of liability.

sections.title: Release on ground of illness.
sections.raw_text:
(1) At any time after a warrant for the arrest of a judgment-debtor has been issued the Court may cancel it on the ground of his serious illness.
(2) Where a judgment-debtor has been arrested, the Court may release him if, in its opinion, he is not in a fit state of health to be detained in the civil prison.
(3) Where a judgment-debtor has been committed to the civil prison, he may be released therefrom—
(a) by the State Government, on the ground of the existence of any infectious or contagious disease, or
(b) by the committing Court, or any Court to which that Court is subordinate, on the ground of his suffering from any serious illness.

breakdown.plain_summary: Illness-based relief is available at every stage of the arrest-and-detention process: before arrest (cancelling the warrant), immediately upon arrest (release if unfit for civil prison), and even after commitment to civil prison (release by the State Government for infectious disease, or by the court for serious illness).
essential_elements: A yet-unexecuted arrest warrant can be cancelled by the court on the ground of the judgment-debtor's serious illness.
An arrested but not-yet-committed judgment-debtor may be released if the court finds him unfit for civil-prison detention.
A judgment-debtor already committed to civil prison may be released by the State Government (infectious/contagious disease) or by the committing court or its superior court (serious illness).
breakdown.how_to_read: A humane safety-valve running through the whole arrest-and-detention pipeline — useful to invoke at whichever stage the judgment-debtor's health becomes an issue, not just at the outset.

sections.title: Property liable to attachment and sale in execution of decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 60 is the master list defining what property of a judgment-debtor can be seized and sold to satisfy a decree — essentially everything of value the debtor owns or can dispose of for their own benefit — and then carves out a long, deliberately protective list of exemptions covering basic necessities (clothing, cooking vessels, tools of trade), a portion of salary and wages, pensions, insurance proceeds, provident fund deposits, and other categories Parliament considered too essential to seize. Crucially, a debtor cannot contractually waive these protections in advance.
essential_elements: Attachable property broadly covers all movable and immovable saleable property belonging to, or beneficially disposable by, the judgment-debtor.

The proviso lists specific exempt categories (a) through (p): basic necessities, tools of trade for agriculturists/artisans, certain dwellings, books of account, mere rights to sue, rights of personal service, pensions/gratuities, wages, a protected slice of salary, armed-forces pay, provident fund deposits, life insurance proceeds, protected tenancies, notified allowances, contingent/expectant interests, future maintenance rights, and other legally exempted allowances.

Salary is only partly attachable: the first slice plus two-thirds of the remainder is exempt (one-third exempt only, i.e. two-thirds attachable, for maintenance decrees), with a further tapering exemption once attachment has run for two years.
Sub-section (1A) voids any agreement by which a judgment-debtor purports to waive these exemptions in advance.
Sub-section (2) clarifies that the housing exemption in clause (c) does not protect against execution of a decree for rent on that very property.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The exemptions are calibrated differently for maintenance decrees (only one-third of salary exempt, i.e. more is attachable) than for other decrees (larger exempt slice).
State Amendments (e.g., Kerala) can add further exempt categories to the clause (g)-style pension list.
breakdown.how_to_read: The single most consulted execution provision in practice — when resisting or planning an attachment, always check clause (a)-(p) first; the salary-attachment mechanics in clause (i)/(ia) plus Explanations I-II are a frequent litigation flashpoint in maintenance-decree enforcement.

sections.title: Partial exemption of agricultural produce.
sections.raw_text: The State Government may, by general or special order published in the Official Gazette, declare that such portion of agricultural produce, or of any class of agricultural produce, as may appear to the State Government to be necessary for the purpose of providing until the next harvest for the due cultivation of the land and for the support of the judgment-debtor and his family, shall, in the case of all agriculturists or of any class of agriculturists, be exempted from liability to attachment or sale in execution of a decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: The State Government can shield a portion of a farmer judgment-debtor's crop from attachment, specifically the amount needed to keep farming until the next harvest and to feed the family in the meantime, by issuing a Gazette order.
essential_elements: Exemption is created only by a State Government order, general or special, published in the Official Gazette.
The exempted quantity is whatever the State Government considers necessary for continued cultivation and family support until the next harvest.
Can apply to all agriculturists or to a specified class of agriculturists.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The exemption is not self-executing — it depends entirely on an actual Gazette notification being issued; absent one, Section 60(1)(b)'s cross-reference to this section has no separate operative content.
breakdown.how_to_read: Operates as a delegated-legislation supplement to Section 60(1)(b)'s agricultural-produce exemption; always check whether the relevant State has actually issued such an order before relying on it.

sections.title: Seizure of property in dwelling-house.
sections.raw_text:
(1) No person executing any process under this Code directing or authorizing seizure of movable property shall enter any dwelling-house after sunset and before sunrise.
(2) No outer door of a dwelling-house shall be broken open unless such dwelling-house is in the occupancy of the judgment-debtor and he refuses or in any way prevents access thereto, but when the person executing any such process has duly gained access to any dwelling-house, he may break open the door of any room in which he has reason to believe any such property to be.
(3) Where a room in a dwelling-house is in the actual occupancy of a woman who, according to the customs of the country, does not appear in public, the person executing the process shall give notice to such woman that she is at liberty to withdraw; and, after allowing reasonable time for her to withdraw and giving her reasonable facility for withdrawing, he may enter such room for the purpose of seizing the property, using at the same time every precaution, consistent with these provisions, to prevent its clandestine removal.

breakdown.plain_summary: This mirrors the dwelling-house entry safeguards for arrest (Section 55) but for seizing movable property in execution: no night-time entry, no breaking open doors except where the debtor refuses access, and special notice-and-withdrawal protection for women observing purdah.
essential_elements: No entry into a dwelling-house between sunset and sunrise for the purpose of seizing movable property.

Outer doors may only be broken open where the judgment-debtor occupies the house and refuses or obstructs access; once access is gained, doors of rooms believed to contain the property may be broken open.

A woman in purdah occupying a room must be given notice and reasonable opportunity to withdraw before entry, with precautions taken against the property being clandestinely removed during the process.
breakdown.how_to_read: A direct structural parallel to Section 55's arrest safeguards, applied instead to seizure of movable property — useful to cite together when challenging execution-process irregularities in the debtor's home.

sections.title: Property attached in execution of decrees of several Courts.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where property not in the custody of any Court is under attachment in execution of decrees of more Courts than one, the Court which shall receive or realize such property and shall determine any claim thereto and any objection to the attachment thereof shall be the Court of highest grade, or, where there is no difference in grade between such Courts, the Court under whose decree the property was first attached.
(2) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to invalidate any proceeding taken by a Court executing one of such decrees.
Explanation.—For the purposes of sub-section (2), "proceeding taken by a Court" does not include an order allowing, to a decree-holder who has purchased property at a sale held in execution of a decree, set off to the extent of the purchase price payable by him.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the same property (not already in any court's custody) is attached by more than one court under different decrees, only one court gets to actually receive/realize the property and resolve claims and objections about it — the highest-grade court, or, if the courts are equal in grade, whichever court attached first.
essential_elements: Applies only to property not already in the custody of any court.
Where multiple courts have attached the same property under different decrees, priority for receiving/realizing it and deciding related claims/objections goes to the highest-grade court.
If the attaching courts are of equal grade, priority goes to whichever court attached the property first.

Earlier proceedings taken by any of the executing courts remain valid despite this priority rule, except a set-off order in favour of a decree-holder who purchased property at auction, which is excluded from that protection.
breakdown.how_to_read: A jurisdiction-traffic-control rule for multi-decree attachments — decisive in determining which court a claimant should approach when several courts have attached the same asset.

sections.title: Private alienation of property after attachment to be void.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where an attachment has been made, any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any interest therein and any payment to the judgment-debtor of any debt, dividend or other monies contrary to such attachment, shall be void as against all claims enforceable under the attachment.
(2) Nothing in this section shall apply to any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any interest therein, made in pursuance of any contract for such transfer or delivery entered into and registered before the attachment.
Explanation.—For the purpose of this section, claims enforceable under an attachment include claims for the rateable distribution of assets.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once property is attached, the judgment-debtor cannot secretly sell, transfer, or hand it over to someone else, nor can a third party pay the debtor money owed to them in a way that defeats the attachment — any such attempt is void against attachment claims. The one carve-out is a transfer made under a contract that was both entered into and registered before the attachment happened.
essential_elements: Applies to private transfers or delivery of attached property (or any interest in it), and to payments of debts/dividends/monies to the judgment-debtor made contrary to the attachment.
Such transfers/payments are void as against all claims enforceable under the attachment, including claims for rateable distribution of assets.
Exception: a transfer made under a contract that was both entered into and registered before the attachment is unaffected.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The registered-contract exception is narrow — it requires both execution and registration of the contract to predate the attachment, not merely an informal prior agreement.
breakdown.how_to_read: The anti-evasion backbone of the attachment regime — pair with Section 63's Explanation on rateable distribution and with Order XXI's attachment procedure when advising a decree-holder worried about the debtor dissipating assets.

sections.title: Purchaser's title.
sections.raw_text: Where immovable property is sold in execution of a decree and such sale has become absolute, the property shall be deemed to have vested in the purchaser from the time when the property is sold and not from the time when the sale becomes absolute.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once an execution sale of immovable property is confirmed (becomes absolute), the law treats the purchaser as having owned the property from the moment of the actual sale — not merely from the later date of confirmation — giving the purchaser's title retroactive effect back to the sale date.
essential_elements: Applies to sales of immovable property in execution of a decree.
Operative only once the sale has become absolute (i.e., confirmed under the applicable execution rules).
Title is deemed to vest in the purchaser retroactively from the date of sale, not from the later date of confirmation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Important for tracing title disputes and for computing limitation/possession periods in cases involving auction-purchased immovable property — the relevant date is the sale date, not the confirmation date.

sections.title: [Suit purchase being on behalf of plaintiff.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1988 (45 of 1988), section 7, with effect from 19 May 1988. This section formerly dealt with the position where property was purchased at an execution sale in the name of one person but on behalf of another (a decree-holder), including restrictions on suits challenging the real ownership of such purchases.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 66 is no longer in force. It used to regulate suits challenging benami-style execution-sale purchases made nominally in one person's name but actually on behalf of the decree-holder or another.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 19 May 1988.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: A stub entry preserving section-number contiguity — do not cite this as live law.

sections.title: Power for State Government to make rules as to sales of land in execution of decrees for payment of money.
sections.raw_text:
(1) The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for any local area imposing conditions in respect of the sale of any class of interests in land in execution of decrees for the payment of money, where such interests are so uncertain or undetermined as, in the opinion of the State Government, to make it impossible to fix their value.
(2) When on the date on which this Code came into operation in any local area, any special rules as to sale of land in execution of decrees were in force therein, the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare such rules to be in force, or may by a like notification, modify the same. Every notification issued in the exercise of the powers conferred by this sub-section shall set out the rules so continued or modified.
(3) Every rule made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before the State Legislature.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the value of a land interest is too uncertain or undetermined to fix normally (making an ordinary sale-in-execution impractical), the State Government can make special rules by Gazette notification governing how such interests are sold to satisfy money decrees, and can continue or modify any pre-existing local special rules on the same subject.
essential_elements: Power applies specifically to interests in land whose uncertainty/indeterminacy makes valuation impossible, in the State Government's opinion.
Rules are made by notification in the Official Gazette and apply to a specified local area.
Pre-existing special local sale rules in force when the Code commenced may be continued or modified by similar notification.
Every rule made under this section must be laid before the State Legislature.
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow rule-making power for an edge case (unvaluable land interests) — mostly relevant in areas with unusual tenurial arrangements; check for a State-specific notification before assuming ordinary Order XXI sale procedure applies.

sections.title: [Power to prescribe rules for transferring to collector execution of certain decrees.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section, together with Sections 69 to 72, formerly formed a scheme permitting execution of certain decrees against immovable property to be transferred to the Collector for execution under special rules, rather than through the ordinary civil court process.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 68 is no longer in force. It used to let the State Government make rules transferring execution of certain decrees against immovable property to the Collector instead of the civil court.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1957.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of a now wholly repealed Collector-execution scheme (Sections 68-72) — see the repeal notes on Sections 69-72 for the rest of the scheme.

sections.title: [Provisions of Third Schedule to apply.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section formerly applied the Code's Third Schedule (governing procedure for Collector-executed decrees) to executions transferred to the Collector under the since-repealed Section 68 scheme.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 69 is no longer in force. It used to apply special Third Schedule procedure to decrees whose execution had been transferred to the Collector.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1957.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of the repealed Collector-execution scheme — see Sections 68, 70, 71, 72.

sections.title: [Rules of Procedure.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section formerly empowered rule-making for the procedure to be followed by Collectors executing decrees transferred to them under the since-repealed Section 68 scheme.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 70 is no longer in force. It used to allow procedural rules to be made for Collectors executing transferred decrees.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1957.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of the repealed Collector-execution scheme — see Sections 68, 69, 71, 72.

sections.title: [Jurisdiction of Civil Courts barred.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section formerly barred civil courts from entertaining matters that fell within the Collector's execution jurisdiction under the since-repealed Section 68 scheme.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 71 is no longer in force. It used to oust civil court jurisdiction over matters assigned to the Collector under the repealed execution-transfer scheme.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1957.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of the repealed Collector-execution scheme — see Sections 68, 69, 70, 72.

sections.title: [Collector to be deemed to be acting judicially.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section formerly deemed a Collector executing a transferred decree under the since-repealed Section 68 scheme to be acting judicially, for purposes such as immunity and procedural protection.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 72 is no longer in force. It used to treat a Collector executing a transferred decree as acting in a judicial capacity.

sections.title: Proceeds of execution-sale to be rateably distributed among decree-holders.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where assets are held by a Court and more persons than one have, before the receipt of such assets, made application to the Court for the execution of decrees for the payment of money passed against the same judgment-debtor and have not obtained satisfaction thereof, the assets, after deducting the costs of realization, shall be rateably distributed among all such persons:
Provided as follows:—
(a) where any property is sold subject to a mortgage or charge, the mortgagee or incumbrancer shall not be entitled to share in any surplus arising from such sale;
(b) where any property liable to be sold in execution of a decree is subject to a mortgage or charge, the Court may, with the consent of the mortgagee or incumbrancer, order that the property be sold free from the mortgage or charge, giving to the mortgagee or incumbrancer the same interest in the proceeds of the sale as he had in the property sold;
(c) where any immovable property is sold in execution of a decree ordering its sale for the discharge of an incumbrance thereon, the proceeds of sale shall be applied — First, in defraying the expenses of the sale; Secondly, in discharging the amount due under the decree; Thirdly, in discharging the interest and principal monies due on subsequent incumbrances (if any); and Fourthly, rateably among the holders of decrees for the payment of money against the judgment-debtor, who have, prior to the sale of the property, applied to the Court which passed the decree ordering such sale for execution of such decrees, and have not obtained satisfaction thereof.
(2) Where all or any of the assets liable to be rateably distributed under this section are paid to a person not entitled to receive the same, any person so entitled may sue such person to compel him to refund the assets.
(3) Nothing in this section affects any right of the Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a court is holding money recovered from a judgment-debtor and several different decree-holders (with separate money decrees against that same debtor) have all applied for execution before the money came in, the court doesn't pay whoever applied first in full — it divides the assets proportionately (rateably) among all of them, after deducting realization costs. Special rules apply where the property was mortgaged or charged.
essential_elements: Applies where a court holds assets and multiple decree-holders, each with unsatisfied money decrees against the same judgment-debtor, applied for execution before those assets were received.
After deducting realization costs, the assets are distributed rateably (proportionately) among all such applicants.
A mortgagee/incumbrancer whose secured property was sold does not share in any surplus from that sale (proviso (a)).
With the mortgagee's consent, property may be sold free of the mortgage, with the mortgagee's interest shifting to the sale proceeds instead (proviso (b)).

Where property is sold specifically to discharge an incumbrance, proceeds go first to sale expenses, then the decree amount, then subsequent incumbrances, and only then rateably among other money-decree holders who applied before the sale (proviso (c)).
A person who wrongly receives assets that should have been rateably distributed can be sued by the rightful claimant to compel a refund.
The section does not affect any right of the Government (which retains its own priority elsewhere in law).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rateable distribution requires the competing applications to have been made before the assets were actually received by the court — later applicants do not automatically share.
breakdown.how_to_read: The key equitable-sharing rule among competing money-decree holders — read with Section 63 (multi-court attachment priority) and Section 64 (void private alienation) as the trio governing multi-claimant execution scenarios.

sections.title: Resistance to execution.
sections.raw_text: Where the Court is satisfied that the holder of a decree for the possession of immovable property or that the purchaser of immovable property sold in execution of a decree has been resisted or obstructed in obtaining possession of the property by the judgment-debtor or some person on his behalf and that such resistance or obstruction was without any just cause, the Court may, at the instance of the decree-holder or purchaser, order the judgment-debtor or such other person to be detained in the civil prison for a term which may extend to thirty days and may further direct that the decree-holder or purchaser be put into possession of the property.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a judgment-debtor (or someone acting for them) blocks the decree-holder or auction-purchaser from actually taking possession of immovable property they're legally entitled to, and the court finds this obstruction had no genuine justification, the court can jail the obstructor for up to thirty days and order that the decree-holder or purchaser be physically given possession.
essential_elements: Applies to resistance or obstruction in obtaining possession of immovable property, whether by a decree-holder or an execution-sale purchaser.
The resistance/obstruction must be by the judgment-debtor or someone acting on their behalf.
The court must be satisfied the resistance was without any just cause.
Remedy: detention in civil prison for up to thirty days, plus a direction to put the decree-holder/purchaser into possession.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the resistance has a genuine/just cause (e.g. a bona fide third-party claim), this coercive remedy is not available — the matter typically proceeds through the investigation machinery in Order XXI instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: A frontline remedy for obstructive judgment-debtors in possession decrees — read alongside Order XXI Rules 97-103, which supply the fuller procedural machinery for resistance and dispossession disputes.

sections.title: Power of Court to issue commissions.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 75 opens Part III's 'Incidental Proceedings' by giving courts a general power to delegate specific fact-finding or administrative tasks to a court-appointed commissioner — from examining witnesses and investigating sites, to auditing accounts, dividing property, running expert investigations, selling perishable goods in custody, or handling routine ministerial acts.
essential_elements: The power to issue a commission is subject to prescribed conditions and limitations (fleshed out in Order XXVI).

Seven distinct purposes are listed: examining a person, local investigation, examining/adjusting accounts, partition, scientific/technical/expert investigation, sale of speedily-decaying property in court custody, and ministerial acts.
breakdown.how_to_read: The gateway provision for Order XXVI's detailed commission procedure — useful whenever a fact-finding task (site inspection, accounts, expert opinion) needs a court-appointed intermediary rather than direct oral evidence.
